docs.title: What is amos?
docs.text:
Automated Modeling for Open Scholarship. \ Like the Rocinante's mechanic in The Expanse, amos makes the dirty jobs of a data science project (cleaning, describing, munging, preprocessing, modeling, evaluating, and visualizing) easier.

You describe a study in a plain settings file (or a Python dict). amos builds the workflow with chrisjen, runs it on your data, compares every combination of the methods you list, and records everything needed to reproduce the result.

docs.title: Accessible
docs.text:
amos is accessible to researchers at all levels. It uses one vocabulary for every stage of a project. A project is made of workers (its stages), which use techniques (the actual methods), sometimes organized in steps. The settings file only names things, so it doubles as a readable description of your methods:

Metrics, such as roc_auc and rmse, are not steps. Techniques use them: a worker's criterion picks the best combination of techniques with one, and the scorecard and validators report them (see the catalog).

The stages are only a convention: any technique can be used in any worker, and you can name your workers whatever you like. And, any step can include none, which tests whether a technique changes the result versus doing nothing at all.

You do not even have to name the techniques. A named pipeline, such as pipeline = classification or pipeline = regression_inference, fills in the analyst, critic, and artist for a kind of study, and adapts to your data as it runs: it fills missing values, encodes categories with many levels differently from those with few, balances rare classes, and chooses the models, evaluators, and figures that suit the data, recording why. Any setting you write yourself wins.

docs.title: Reproducible
docs.text:
Open scholarship means that others can check your work. amos helps by:

  • Passing one seed to every tool that takes a random_state, so a project yields the same result every time.
  • Applying a project to a copy of your data, so running it twice gives the same answer and your data is never changed.
  • Keeping a history of every technique that was applied, with the exact tool and parameters it used.
  • Isolating training and testing data. Every scaler, encoder, imputer, and sampler is fitted to the training rows and then applied to the test rows, so nothing leaks from the test set.
  • All settings and parameters can be implemented through a single settings file that will produce the same results on any computer.

docs.title: Flexible
docs.text:
amos wraps the major Python data science packages behind one interface, so you can compare their methods side by side without learning each package's quirks:

Package What amos uses it for scikit-learn Splitting, imputing, scaling, feature selection, models, cross-validation, metrics, and permutation importance. category_encoders and skrub Target, weight of evidence, and a dozen other data encoders. imbalanced-learn SMOTE and other ways to balance the classes of the training rows. xgboost, lightgbm, and catboost Gradient boosting. InterpretML Explainable boosting machines: accurate models whose every effect can be shown. TabPFN A pretrained model that is most accurate on small data. Optuna Hyperparameter searches that learn from each try. statsmodels and pyfixest Regressions with standard errors, p-values, and confidence intervals: least squares, generalized linear, quantile, robust, mixed, and GEE models; models of counts, of two or more classes, and of ordered classes; fixed effects and clustered standard errors; and principal component and factor analysis of the features. Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression of the time until an event. DoubleML, DoWhy, causalml, and tigramite Causal inference: the effects of a treatment, estimated with double machine learning, regression, matching, weighting, instruments, regression discontinuities, and meta-learners, and causal discovery in time series. fairlearn Fairness metrics that compare a model across groups. MAPIE Conformal prediction: intervals and sets with a known rate of coverage. shap and eli5 Explaining models with SHAP values (and shap's plots of them) and weights. dtreeviz Plots of decision trees: the rows in each leaf, the splits across features, and the path of one row. mlxtend Sequential and exhaustive searches for the best features, association rules, the bias-variance decomposition, and plots of decision regions. matplotlib, seaborn, and SciencePlots Figures and other visualizations, in the style of a scientific journal (Nature's, by default) and with colors that people with color blindness can tell apart. great_tables and python-docx Scorecards as HTML tables and Word documents.

docs.title: Robust and Transparent
docs.text:
A result that depends on one arbitrary choice of preprocessing or model is fragile. The experiment design tries every combination of the techniques you list for each step and reports how each one did, so readers can see that your conclusions are robust (or not). The critic's scorecard puts every combination side by side, on every metric, in a table (as csv, Markdown, LaTeX, HTML, Word, or an image).

Name the columns that identify groups as groups, and amos keeps them out of the model's features while it uses them to check fairness across groups, to add fixed effects and cluster standard errors, and to keep each group in one set when it splits the data.

docs.title: Extensible
docs.text:
Every technique is a small Python class that is added to a library as soon as it is defined, so it can be named in settings right away. To wrap a tool that amos does not include, name its import path:

import amos

transformer = amos.Transformer(
    name = "yeo_johnson", contents = "sklearn.preprocessing.PowerTransformer")
print(transformer.name)
# yeo_johnson

You can use any naming convention you like, but, by default, amos uses snakecase of a class name as the default key for accessing it from the stored technique library.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
amos requires Python 3.11 or later. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows. It is built on chrisjen, numpy, pandas, and scikit-learn, which are installed automatically.

On a computer with an NVIDIA GPU, set use_gpu = true in the "general" section of the settings, and the xgboost, catboost, lightgbm, and tabpfn models are fitted on the GPU (and on the CPU if there is none). It is false by default. See fitting models on a GPU.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To install amos, use pip:

pip install amos

The other packages that amos wraps are optional. A technique imports its package only when it is used, and tells you which extra to install if the package is missing. Install them all (except TabPFN) with pip install amos[all], or choose:

Extra Installs For boosting xgboost, lightgbm, catboost Gradient boosting models. causal DoubleML (with rdrobust), tigramite, causalml (on Python 3.11 and 3.12), DoWhy (on Python 3.13 and later) Inferers for causal inference, such as partially_linear, regression_discontinuity, propensity_matching, x_learner, and pcmci. encoders category_encoders, skrub Target encoders, and encoders for text and dates. explain shap, eli5, InterpretML, dtreeviz shap_importance, the SHAP plots (such as shap_beeswarm), explain_weights, explainable_boosting, and dtreeviz's plots of trees (such as tree_leaf_sizes). fairness fairlearn Fairness metrics and the fairness table. mlxtend mlxtend sequential_selection, exhaustive_selection, association_rules, bias_variance, and decision_regions. plots matplotlib, seaborn, SciencePlots The artist's figures, and scorecards and regression tables as images. polars Polars, pyarrow Reading Polars data frames. sampling imbalanced-learn Samplers such as smote. statistics statsmodels, pyfixest ols, glm, logit_sm, fixest, and the other models with inference (such as poisson, probit, and mixedlm). survival statsmodels cox, kaplan_meier, survival_curves, and concordance. tables great_tables Scorecards and regression tables as HTML tables. tuning Optuna search = "optuna" for any model. uncertainty MAPIE conformal intervals and sets. word python-docx Scorecards and regression tables as Word documents. tabpfn TabPFN The tabpfn model. It needs PyTorch, which is large, so it is not part of all.

docs.title: Describe your study
docs.text:
Most users describe a study in a settings file. This is a study of the Wisconsin breast cancer data that uses every stage, as an ini file:

[general]
seed = 43
label = target

[cancer_project]
cancer_workers = wrangler, explorer, analyst, critic, artist

[wrangler]
techniques = drop_duplicates, drop_constant

[explorer]
techniques = summarize, missing_values, label_balance

[analyst]
design = experiment
criterion = roc_auc
steps = split, scale, sample, model
split_techniques = stratified
scale_techniques = standard, min_max
sample_techniques = none, smote
model_techniques = logit, random_forest, xgboost

[critic]
techniques = scorecard, confusion, permutation_importance

[artist]
techniques = roc_curve, importance_plot, confusion_heatmap, shap_waterfall

[random_forest_parameters]
n_estimators = 100

[roc_curve_parameters]
title = How well the best model separates the classes

[importance_plot_parameters]
title = The ten features that matter most
limit = 10

[confusion_heatmap_parameters]
title = The test rows by their actual and predicted classes

[shap_waterfall_parameters]
title = How each feature moved the prediction for one tumor
limit = 30
height = 10

The "general" section names the label (the column that models predict) and the seed. The project section lists the workers. In the "analyst", each {step}_techniques setting lists alternatives, and the experiment design tries every combination: 2 scalers, 2 samplers, and 3 models (scikit-learn's logistic regression, a random forest, and xgboost's gradient boosting) make 12 combinations. Parameters for any technique go in a {technique}_parameters section. The study uses optional packages (imbalanced-learn for smote, xgboost, shap for shap_waterfall, and matplotlib, seaborn, and SciencePlots for the figures), which pip install amos[all] installs.

This is the workflow that amos builds from those settings. The workers run in order, and the analyst tries every path through its steps:

flowchart TB
    data[("breast cancer data")] --> wrangler

    subgraph wrangler ["wrangler"]
        direction LR
        drop_duplicates --> drop_constant
    end

    subgraph explorer ["explorer"]
        direction LR
        summarize --> missing_values --> label_balance
    end

    subgraph analyst ["analyst: an experiment of 12 combinations"]
        direction LR
        subgraph split ["split"]
            stratified
        end
        subgraph scale ["scale"]
            standard
            min_max
        end
        subgraph sample ["sample"]
            none
            smote
        end
        subgraph model ["model"]
            logit
            random_forest
            xgboost
        end
        split --> scale --> sample --> model
    end

    subgraph critic ["critic"]
        direction LR
        scorecard --> confusion --> permutation_importance
    end

    subgraph artist ["artist"]
        direction LR
        roc_curve --> importance_plot --> confusion_heatmap --> shap_waterfall
    end

    wrangler --> explorer --> analyst
    analyst -- "the combination with the best roc_auc" --> critic
    critic --> artist

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Pass the settings and the data (a pandas.DataFrame, a path to a data file in any format that nagata reads, such as csv, Excel, parquet, Stata, SAS, or SPSS, or a scikit-learn dataset) to Project.create:

import sklearn.datasets

import amos

cancer = sklearn.datasets.load_breast_cancer(as_frame = True)
project = amos.Project.create("cancer.ini", item = cancer, id = "first_run")
result = project.result
print(result.metrics["roc_auc"] > 0.95)
# True
print(sorted(result.figures))
# ['confusion_heatmap', 'importance_plot', 'roc_curve', 'shap_waterfall']

The artist drew four figures, titled by their {technique}_parameters sections. The ROC curve shows how well the best combination tells the two kinds of tumors apart on the test rows it never learned from, and the confusion heatmap counts the test rows that it classified rightly and wrongly. The importance plot shows how much its score drops when each feature is shuffled, which works for any model, and the SHAP waterfall shows how every feature (after scaling) moved its prediction for one tumor:

The result includes a Dataset, the fitted model, its predictions, metrics, tables, figures, and the history of every technique.

The settings can also say where the data comes from. A loader in the wrangler (load_file, download, or openml) loads a data file, or downloads one first, with the project's file manager, and then the project needs no item. See loading data.

docs.title: Compare every branch
docs.text:
The critic's scorecard compares every branch of the analysis: each combination of techniques that the experiment tried, ranked by the criterion, with every standard metric for the task computed from that branch's own predictions on the test rows. It can be saved as a csv file, a Markdown table, a Word document, or an image:

scorecard = project.scorecard
print(len(scorecard.table), list(scorecard.table.columns[:5]))
# 12 ['rank', 'split', 'scale', 'sample', 'model']
scorecard.to_csv("scorecard.csv")
scorecard.to_markdown("scorecard.md")
scorecard.to_word("scorecard.docx")
scorecard.to_image("scorecard.png")

This is the scorecard of the study, saved as an image. The best branch is shaded:

docs.title: Report the estimates
docs.text:
A regression_table reports models the way Stata reports a regression: for each model, the number of observations and its fit statistics, then each feature's estimate, standard error, test statistic, p-value, and 95% confidence interval. Most machine learning models have no coefficients with standard errors, so amos reports each feature's average marginal effect (Stata's "dy/dx") instead: the average change in the prediction (here, the predicted probability of a benign tumor) for a one-unit increase in the feature. Its standard error comes from refitting the model to 100 bootstrap samples of the training rows. The fit statistics are cross-validated, since a flexible model can fit the rows that it learned from almost perfectly. Models that report their own coefficients and standard errors, such as ols and logit_sm, show those instead.

Every branch of the experiment is fitted and kept in memory, so the best logistic regression and the best boosted trees can each be reported, and saved as a Word document or an image:

branches = sorted(result.branches, key = lambda branch: branch.score, reverse = True)
tables = {}
for model in ("logit", "xgboost"):
    dataset = next(b.dataset for b in branches if b.steps["model"] == model)
    tables[model] = amos.evaluators.RegressionTable.create(
        {model: dataset}, title = f"The best {model} branch")
    tables[model].to_word(f"regression_{model}.docx")
    tables[model].to_image(f"regression_{model}.png")
print(tables["logit"].to_text().splitlines()[0].split())
# ['logit', 'Number', 'of', 'obs', '=', '426']
print(tables["logit"].estimates.loc[("logit", "mean radius"), "estimate"].round(3))
# -0.012

These are the two images. to_text prints the same table, and one table can hold several models: as a block for each in Word documents and images, or side by side, with stars, in csv, Markdown, LaTeX, and HTML.

The best logit branch scaled the features with standard and the best xgboost branch with min_max and smote. So one unit is a standard deviation of the feature for logit and the feature's whole range for xgboost. Read the signs, p-values, and fit statistics across the tables, not the sizes of the estimates. Both models find that larger, more irregular cells make a tumor less likely to be benign. The logistic regression is confident about most features. The trees spread their effect over a few correlated "worst" features, so each one's effect is uncertain on its own, and a feature that no tree splits on has an effect of exactly 0.

docs.title: Export the results
docs.text:
export saves everything needed to report and reproduce the results in a folder named for the run. The project's clerk (an amos.Clerk) keeps data and results outside your code, in the "data" and "studies" folders beside the "code" folder that holds it.

There is much more to amos, including hyperparameter searches, statistical inference with statsmodels, every technique and its parameters, and how to write your own. See the documentation, especially the tutorial, the advanced user guide, the technique catalog, and the recipes.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributors are always welcome. Feel free to grab an issue to work on or make a suggested improvement. If you wish to contribute, please read the Contribution Guide and Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Similar Projects
docs.text:
• scikit-learn: its Pipeline and GridSearchCV combine preprocessing and models and search over hyperparameters. amos uses scikit-learn throughout, and adds named columns, supervised encoders, samplers, comparisons of whole combinations of methods, and settings files.
  • PyCaret: a low-code library that compares many models with a few function calls. It automates more choices for you, while amos asks you to list your methods so that they can be reported.
  • Kedro: a framework for reproducible data pipelines, with more structure for large, long-running projects.
  • MLflow and DVC: track experiments, data, and models over time. They work well alongside amos.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
If you use amos in your research, please cite it. GitHub's "Cite this repository" button reads the same information from CITATION.cff.

docs.title: Advanced User Guide
docs.text: The tutorial shows how to build a study. This guide describes how amos works, every setting, and how to add your own techniques. The technique catalog lists every technique. Every example on this page is run by the amos unit tests.

docs.title: How the pieces fit together
docs.text:
settings ──create──▶ Idea ──draft──▶ workflow ──apply──▶ Dataset ──▶ report, export
(file or dict)     (chrisjen      (graph of workers,   (your data and
                    settings)      steps, techniques)   all it taught)

amos is built on chrisjen, which reads settings and builds a workflow from them. Everything that chrisjen does works in amos, so its advanced guide applies here too. amos adds:

Class Description Project A chrisjen.Project that makes your data into a Dataset, applies the workflow to a copy of it, and can export the results. Dataset The item that flows through the workflow: the data, the label, the split, the model, and everything learned. Operation Base class for every amos technique (a chrisjen.Technique that works on a Dataset). Loader, Cleaner, Munger, Merger, Shaper, Describer, Splitter, Transformer, Sampler, Model, Validator, Evaluator, Inferer, Plot The genres of techniques. Transformer has the genres Imputer, Scaler, Encoder, Mixer, Selector, and Reducer, and Inferer has a genre for each package of causal inference (Doubleml, Dowhy, Causalml, and Tigramite). Metric Base class for metrics, which score a model's predictions. A metric is a chrisjen.Criteria, not a technique, so it is not a step of a workflow: name it as a criterion, or in the metrics of a technique such as scorecard or a validator. GroupMetric is its genre of fairness metrics. Chooser The genre of the techniques that choose other techniques to suit the data (auto, auto_sampler, auto_model, and auto_plot). See Choosing techniques automatically. Experiment A design that compares every combination of techniques and keeps a table of how each did. Findings The default report.

docs.title: The library
docs.text:
Every technique is a class, stored in the chrisjen library (also available as amos.library) under its snake case name as soon as it is defined. That is how names in settings are found. The genres are nested layers of the library:

import dataclasses

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sklearn.datasets

import amos

print(sorted(amos.library["vertex"]["operation"]))
# ['chooser', 'cleaner', 'describer', 'evaluator', 'inferer', 'loader', 'merger', 'model', 'munger', 'plot', 'sampler', 'shaper', 'splitter', 'transformer', 'validator']
print(amos.library.classify("smote"), amos.library.classify("one_hot"))
# sampler encoder
print(amos.library.all["random_forest"])
# <class 'amos.models.RandomForest'>

Names must be unique across the library, including the names of chrisjen classes such as "none", "flow", and "summary". The technique catalog lists every technique by genre.

docs.title: Settings reference
docs.text:
A project's settings are sections of settings. amos reads three special sections. Every other section is read by chrisjen.

The idea file page shows how to write settings in a file and describes the "general" section in detail.

Section Setting Meaning general label The column that models predict. task "classify" or "regress", if it should not be inferred from the label. seed Seed for every random process (passed as random_state). groups Columns that identify groups of rows (see "Groups and fairness" below). use_gpu Whether to fit the models that can use a GPU (xgboost, catboost, lightgbm, and tabpfn) on an NVIDIA GPU. Defaults to false (see "Fitting models on a GPU" below). conserve_memory Whether every experiment keeps only the best combination's whole dataset, rather than every combination's, while it tries them. A worker's own conserve_memory setting wins. Defaults to false (see "Experiments" below). pipeline A named pipeline (such as classification or regression_inference) that fills in the settings of the analyst, critic, and artist. It can also be in the project's section, or in the section of one of those workers for that worker alone. Settings that you write win. See pipeline. files root_folder The workspace, which the other folders are in. Defaults to the folder that holds the "code" folder (see "Where data and results are kept" below). input_folder Folder (in the root folder) where data files named by a relative path are looked for, and where loaders save downloads. Defaults to "data". data_subfolder The subfolder of the input folder that holds the project's data (such as "crime/nibrs"), which becomes the input folder. interim_folder Folder (in the root folder) for intermediate files. Defaults to the input folder. output_folder Folder (in the root folder) in which export makes a folder for each run. Defaults to "studies". export_results Whether to export the results after every run. Defaults to False. feature_groups {group} The features (columns) in a group, which is then a technique that keeps only them (see "Selecting features" below).

The chrisjen settings, in brief:

Setting Meaning A section named {name}_project The project. Its {name}_workers setting lists the workers, in order. A section named for a worker The worker's settings, below. steps or {name}_steps The steps of the worker (or of name). techniques or {name}_techniques The techniques of the worker (or of the step name). In an experiment, the techniques of a step are alternatives. design or {name}_design How the worker applies its nodes. Defaults to flow. criterion or {name}_criterion What an experiment or contest compares: a metric (such as roc_auc) or another chrisjen.Criteria. A section named {name}_parameters Parameters for the technique, step, or worker name. A section named {technique}_{step}_parameters Parameters for one technique in one step.

The designs:

Design What it does flow Applies its nodes one after another. The default. experiment Tries every combination of one technique from each step, keeps the best, and adds a comparison table. contest Like experiment, without the table. survey Tries every combination and averages the results. The results must be numbers, so it is rarely used with a Dataset. benchmark Repeats its nodes until its criterion is met.

docs.title: Where data and results are kept
docs.text:
A project's clerk is an amos.Clerk (a nagata.FileManager), which keeps the data and results outside the project's code, in the "workspace" that holds the "code" folder:

projects/                (the workspace)
    code/
        my_study/        (the project's code, where it is run)
    data/
        crime/nibrs/     (a project's data, in its own subfolder)
    studies/
        my_study_2026-10-30_09-15-00/   (each run's results)

So data that many projects use is kept once, and neither data nor results have to be left out of a repository by hand. The workspace is the folder that holds the nearest folder named "code" at or above the current folder (or the current folder, if there is none). The environment variable AMOS_WORKSPACE names another, and so does amos.options._DEFAULT_ROOT (for a package built on amos). The "files" section of the settings can name the project's data subfolder and change any folder:

[files]
data_subfolder = "crime/nibrs"

A Clerk can also be made and passed as the clerk of Project.create, for example amos.Clerk(data_subfolder = "crime/nibrs"). Each folder is made if it does not exist.

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text:
A Dataset has these attributes:

Attribute Meaning data The data, a pandas.DataFrame. It stays one DataFrame after the data is split. label The name of the column that models predict. task "classify" or "regress". seed Seed for every random process. groups Columns that identify groups of rows. They stay in the data but are not features. use_gpu Whether the models that can use a GPU are fitted on one. train, test Index labels of the training and test rows. test is None until the data is split. synthetic Index labels of the training rows that a sampler made up (synthetic rows and extra copies of a row). model The fitted model. predictions Predictions for the test rows (or every row, if the data is not split). probabilities Predicted probabilities of each class, for the same rows. metrics Scores, by the name of each metric. tables, figures Tables and figures, by the name of the technique that made them. fitted Fitted tools (such as a scaler), by the name of the technique that fitted them. history A record of each technique applied, with its tool and parameters. branches A record of every branch of the most recent experiment (for the scorecard). kinds The kind that set_kinds gave each column (see "Kinds of columns" below).

A label that is not yet a column is pending until a technique makes it (see "Settings named for columns" below).

Its properties select parts of the data: x and y (the features and the label), x_train, y_train, x_test, and y_test, and the names of the features of each kind:

data = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": [31, 45, 52, 38],
    "court": ["state", "federal", "state", "state"],
    "appealed": [True, False, True, False],
    "decided": pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-02", "2021-03-04", "2022-05-06", "2023-07-08"]),
    "reversed": ["yes", "no", "no", "yes"],
})
dataset = amos.Dataset(data, label = "reversed")
print(dataset.numerics, dataset.categoricals, dataset.booleans, dataset.dates)
# ['age'] ['court'] ['appealed'] ['decided']
print(dataset.task, dataset.classes)
# classify ['no', 'yes']

Models cannot use dates or text, so encode them (dates with date_parts, and text with an encoder such as one_hot or tfidf) or remove them before the model step.

Dataset.create makes a dataset from a DataFrame, a Polars DataFrame or LazyFrame, a numpy array, a dict of columns, the path to a data file, or a scikit-learn dataset loaded with as_frame = True. A Project does this for you. A data file is read just as load_file reads it (see "Loading data" below), so it may be in any format that nagata knows. A project reads it with its clerk, so a relative path is looked for in the current folder and then in the clerk's input folder.

docs.title: Loading data
docs.text:
A loader makes the dataset from a source named in the settings, so a project with a loader needs no item. Loaders are usually the first step of the wrangler. They work through the project's clerk (an amos.Clerk): a file named by a relative path is looked for in the current folder and then in the clerk's input folder (the input_folder of the "files" section), and downloads are saved in the input folder.

Loader Source Other parameters load_file The path of a data file. download The URL of a file (http or https). It is saved in the input folder and only downloaded again if it is missing. file_name (what to save it as), refresh (to download it again), and timeout (in seconds) openml The name (such as "credit-g") or id (such as 31) of an OpenML dataset, which scikit-learn saves in the input folder. Its default target is the label unless "label" is set. version, target_column, and the other parameters of sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml

Every loader takes a source, and the label, task, and groups of the data, which default to those in the "general" section. The dataset's history records the source. This project loads a file from its input folder:

court,appeals,reversed
state,2,yes
federal,1,no
state,2,yes
state,0,no
federal,3,yes
state,1,no

settings = {
    "general": {"label": "reversed", "seed": 43},
    "files": {"input_folder": "data"},
    "cases_project": {"cases_workers": "wrangler, explorer"},
    "wrangler": {
        "steps": "load, clean",
        "load_techniques": "load_file",
        "clean_techniques": "drop_duplicates",
    },
    "load_file_parameters": {"source": "cases.csv"},
    "explorer": {"techniques": "label_balance"},
}
project = amos.Project.create(settings, id = "loaded")
print(project.result)
# Dataset(rows=5, columns=3, label='reversed', task='classify')
print(project.result.history[0])
# {'technique': 'load_file', 'source': 'cases.csv', 'rows': 6, 'columns': 3}

load_file and download load a file in any format that the clerk knows (such as csv, tsv, Excel, parquet, feather, json, json lines, fixed-width, HDF, ORC, XML, Stata, SAS, and SPSS), which they find from the file's extension. A path passed as a project's item, or to Dataset.create, is read the same way. pandas opens a compressed file (such as "cases.csv.gz") itself. Set file_format (such as "csv") for a file whose name does not say what it is, and member to load one file from a zip archive, which is extracted to a folder named for the archive. Other parameters, such as sep, go to the pandas reader if it accepts them. Unlike the clerk's own defaults (which suit quick tests), loaders read every row and read text as UTF-8, as pandas does.

A file online is named the same way, and is downloaded the first time the project runs:

[wrangler]
steps = load, clean
load_techniques = download
clean_techniques = drop_duplicates

[download_parameters]
source = https://example.com/data/cases.csv.gz

To read another kind of file, add a format to nagata. Every subclass of nagata.base.FileFormat that is not abstract adds itself to nagata's formats when it is defined, named for the class in snake case without "file_format_" (so FileFormatPsv is "psv"). It is then read by load_file, download, the mergers, and a project's item alike:

import dataclasses

import nagata

@dataclasses.dataclass
class FileFormatPsv(nagata.FileFormatCSV):
    """Pipe-separated values."""

    extensions = ("psv",)

    def load(self, path, **kwargs):
        kwargs.setdefault("sep", "|")
        return super().load(path, **kwargs)

pd.DataFrame({"court": ["state", "federal"], "appeals": [2, 1]}).to_csv(
    "appeals.psv", sep = "|", index = False)
print(amos.Dataset.create("appeals.psv"))
# Dataset(rows=2, columns=2)

To write a loader for another source, see "Writing your own techniques" below.

docs.title: Munging data
docs.text:
Cleaners remove rows and columns. Mungers change what is in the columns, or make new columns from them, without adding or removing rows. Each one changes a whole column at once with the vectorized methods of pandas, so they are fast even with a lot of data. None of them learns from the data, so, like cleaners, they belong in the wrangler, before the data is split. The technique catalog describes each one:

Kind Mungers Text strip_text, normalize_text, replace_text Patterns in text flag_patterns, count_patterns, map_patterns, extract_pattern, extract_all, split_text Values and types map_values, parse_numbers, parse_dates, parse_booleans, convert_types, auto_categorize, set_kinds Combining columns coalesce, combine_flags, derive_columns

Many mungers search text for patterns, which are regular expressions. A pattern is found anywhere in the text, so "revers" is found in "Reversed and remanded", and "revers|vacat" finds either word. Characters with special meanings, such as "." and "(", need a backslash to stand for themselves ("F.3d"). Set "ignorecase" to ignore the difference between capital and lower-case letters. Missing text matches nothing.

A munger that searches text reads one column. flag_patterns and count_patterns make a column for each name in their "patterns", and the others make the column in their "name" (or, without one, replace the column they read). Parameters that map names or patterns to values, such as "patterns", need settings that have mappings: a toml, json, or yaml file, or a Python dict (an ini file has none). In toml, text in single quotes keeps its backslashes as they are:

[coding_project]
coding_workers = "wrangler"

[wrangler]
techniques = "split_text, flag_patterns, map_patterns, parse_numbers"

[split_text_parameters]
column = "caption"
pattern = '\s+v\.\s+'
names = ["party1", "party2"]

[flag_patterns_parameters]
column = "caption"

[flag_patterns_parameters.patterns]
government = 'United States|\bState of\b'

[map_patterns_parameters]
column = "disposition"
name = "outcome"
ignorecase = true

[map_patterns_parameters.patterns]
'revers|vacat' = "reversed"
affirm = "affirmed"

[parse_numbers_parameters]
columns = "damages"

opinions = pd.DataFrame({
    "caption": ["United States v. Smith", "Jones v. Acme Corp.", "Doe v. Roe"],
    "disposition": ["REVERSED and remanded", "Affirmed.", "Vacated."],
    "damages": ["$1,200", "n/a", "$350.50"],
})
coding = amos.Project.create("coding.toml", item = opinions)
coded = coding.result.data
print(coded["party1"].tolist(), coded["party2"].tolist())
# ['United States', 'Jones', 'Doe'] ['Smith', 'Acme Corp.', 'Roe']
print(coded["government"].tolist(), coded["outcome"].tolist())
# [True, False, False] ['reversed', 'affirmed', 'reversed']
print(coded["damages"].tolist())
# [1200.0, nan, 350.5]
print(coding.result.history[0])
# {'technique': 'split_text', 'changed': [], 'created': ['party1', 'party2']}

Each munger records the columns whose values or types it changed and the columns it made. Like any technique, a munger can also be applied by hand. A pattern with named groups makes a column of each group:

citations = amos.Dataset(
    pd.DataFrame({"cite": ["512 F.3d 1093", "98 F.4th 12", "unpublished"]}))
amos.mungers.ExtractPattern().apply(
    citations, column = "cite", pattern = r"(?P<volume>\d+) F\.\w+ (?P<page>\d+)")
amos.mungers.ParseNumbers().apply(citations, columns = ["volume", "page"])
print(citations.data["volume"].tolist(), citations.data["page"].tolist())
# [512.0, 98.0, nan] [1093.0, 12.0, nan]

docs.title: Settings named for columns
docs.text:
Some cleaners and mungers take settings named for the columns they are about, so an ini file needs no mappings for them:

Technique A setting name = value means Other settings rename_columns Rename the column name to value. names filter_rows Keep the rows whose name meets the condition value. query derive_columns Make the column name from the expression value. expressions set_kinds Give the columns in value the kind name (see below). none

A condition of filter_rows starts with a comparison ("", "!=", "<", "<=", ">", ">=", "in", or "not in"). "not" and a value (as in "not 1") means "!=", a list means "in", and a value alone means "". The rows kept meet every condition (and the query, if there is one). In the conditions and in the expressions of derive_columns, a word that is not a column is a value, so text needs no quotes: "offender_race == B" is "offender_race == 'B'". If a word is both a column and a value of the column it is compared to, it raises an error; put the value in quotes or the column in backticks.

The label can be a column that the wrangler makes. Until a technique makes it, the label is pending: the dataset keeps its name, and its task is inferred once the column is made.

[general]
label = won  # made by derive_columns

[wrangle_project]
wrangle_workers = wrangler

[wrangler]
techniques = rename_columns, filter_rows, derive_columns,
    set_kinds

[rename_columns_parameters]
court_type = court

[filter_rows_parameters]
court = not in [tax, bankruptcy]
damages = > 0

[derive_columns_parameters]
won = outcome in [reversed, vacated]
federal = court == federal

[set_kinds_parameters]
dummy = federal
categorical = court

appeals = pd.DataFrame({
    "court_type": ["federal", "state", "tax", "federal", "state"],
    "damages": [100.0, 2500.0, 40.0, 0.0, 75.5],
    "outcome": ["reversed", "affirmed", "reversed", "vacated", "vacated"],
})
wrangled = amos.Project.create("wrangle.ini", item = appeals).result
print(wrangled.label, wrangled.task, wrangled.data["won"].tolist())
# won classify [1, 0, 1]
print(wrangled.data.dtypes.astype(str).to_dict())
# {'court': 'category', 'damages': 'float32', 'outcome': 'category', 'won': 'int8', 'federal': 'int8'}

Since every setting of these techniques other than those in the last column is a column, a parameter set for the whole wrangler (in a "wrangler_parameters" section) would be read as a column. Set their parameters in their own sections.

docs.title: Kinds of columns
docs.text:
set_kinds gives each column a kind, "dummy", "categorical", or "numerical", and stores it in the smallest type that holds its values exactly. A dummy is int8 (0 and 1), and raises an error if it has missing values or any other value. A categorical column is the pandas "category" type. A numerical column is the smallest integer type if its values are whole numbers with none missing, and otherwise float32 (or float64, for numbers that float32 cannot hold to about 7 digits).

Columns that are not listed get the kind of their values: a boolean column or a column of only 0s and 1s is a dummy, other numbers are numerical, and a categorical column or text with few values is categorical. Dates, longer text, and the groups are left as they are. A classified label of booleans (or 0s and 1s) becomes a dummy. The kinds are kept in Dataset.kinds, so a dummy is one of the dataset's booleans even though it holds numbers, and frequencies with columns = all counts the dummies with the categorical columns:

print(wrangled.booleans, wrangled.categoricals, wrangled.numerics)
# ['federal'] ['court', 'outcome'] ['damages']

Arithmetic on small integer types can overflow (int8 holds only -128 to 127), so make new columns from numbers before setting their kinds.

docs.title: Maps of values
docs.text:
map_values replaces values with others, as its "values" map says. Without "values", it uses the map (or function) registered for each of its "columns" with amos.register_value_map, so a package built on amos can register the meanings of its codes once and its projects only name the columns:

amos.register_value_map(["offender_race", "victim_race"], {"W": "white", "B": "black"})
crimes = amos.Dataset(pd.DataFrame({
    "offender_race": ["W", "B", "B"],
    "victim_race": ["B", "B", "W"],
    "age": [19, 34, 52],
}))
amos.mungers.MapValues().apply(crimes, columns = ["offender_race", "victim_race"])
print(crimes.data["offender_race"].tolist())
# ['white', 'black', 'black']

The order of the wrangler's techniques is up to you: a technique after map_values sees the new values, not the codes.

docs.title: Merging data
docs.text:
Research often needs data from sources that are not organized the same way: one table has a row for each case, and another has a row for each court, or for each court that each judge has served on. A merger matches each row of the data to a row of another table and adds that row's columns. The mergers differ in how they match rows (the technique catalog lists them):

Merger A row of the data gets Its parameters merge_keys The columns of the row with the same keys (such as its court). on, other_on, ignorecase, and duplicates merge_nearest The columns of the row with the nearest date or number (such as the last rating of its court before it was decided). column, other_column, direction, tolerance, and keys, if any merge_ranges The columns of the row whose range has its date or number in it (such as the president in office in its year). column, start, end, duplicates, and keys, if any merge_summary Summaries of every row with the same keys (such as the number of judges of its court and the share of them who are women). how, count, and the keys

A merger never adds, removes, or reorders rows. The data keeps the unit that it studies, its label, its groups, and its index, so a merger cannot quietly multiply or lose your observations. A row without a match gets missing values. So start from the table whose rows are what you study (which is the table with the label), and merge the others into it. If the other table describes something else (judges, when the rows of the data are cases), reshape the data first (see reshaping data).

Every merger takes these parameters:

Parameter Meaning source The other table: the path of a data file, which is found and loaded as a loader would (a relative path is looked for in the current folder and then in the clerk's input folder). In Python, it can also be a DataFrame, a Dataset, or anything else that Dataset.create accepts. reader Parameters for loading the file, such as file_format, member, or sep. columns The columns of the other table to add. By default, they are every column whose name the data does not already have (other than the keys of the other table, which repeat those of the data). prefix Text to put before the names of the added columns, such as "judge_". indicator The name of a column to make that says whether each row was matched.

on names the key columns of the data, and other_on those of the other table, if they have other names there. A key must be the same kind of data (numbers, dates, or text) in both tables. Set ignorecase to match text keys without regard to capital letters or the spaces around them. A missing key matches nothing. A row can match only one row, so merge_keys and merge_ranges stop if a row matches several, unless duplicates says to use the "first" or "last" of them (merge_summary summarizes them instead).

The history records how many rows were matched, which is worth checking (and reporting) every time:

court,circuit,judgeships
First Circuit,1,6
Ninth Circuit,9,29
Second Circuit,2,13

rulings = pd.DataFrame({
    "case": ["a1", "a2", "a3", "a4"],
    "court": ["First Circuit", "ninth circuit", "First Circuit", "Tax Court"],
    "year": [2001, 2015, 2019, 2010],
    "reversed": [True, False, True, False],
})
merging = {
    "general": {"label": "reversed"},
    "files": {"input_folder": "data"},
    "rulings_project": {"rulings_workers": "wrangler"},
    "wrangler": {"techniques": "merge_keys"},
    "merge_keys_parameters": {
        "source": "courts.csv",
        "on": "court",
        "ignorecase": True,
        "indicator": "court_found",
    },
}
merged = amos.Project.create(merging, item = rulings).result
print(merged.data["circuit"].tolist(), merged.data["court_found"].tolist())
# [1.0, 9.0, 1.0, nan] [True, True, True, False]
print(merged.history[0])
# {'technique': 'merge_keys', 'source': 'courts.csv', 'rows': 4, 'matched': 3, 'created': ['circuit', 'judgeships', 'court_found']}

merge_ranges and merge_nearest match rows in time. A range has a start and an end (both are in the range), and a missing one means that the range has no limit on that side, as with a term that is still going on. merge_nearest looks "before" a row's date or number unless direction says "after" or "nearest", so that nothing is used that was not yet known, and no farther than tolerance, if it is set:

terms = pd.DataFrame({
    "president": ["Clinton", "Bush", "Obama", "Trump"],
    "began": [1993, 2001, 2009, 2017],
    "ended": [2000, 2008, 2016, 2020],
})
amos.mergers.MergeRanges().apply(
    merged, source = terms, column = "year", start = "began", end = "ended",
    columns = "president")
print(merged.data["president"].tolist())
# ['Bush', 'Obama', 'Trump', 'Obama']

merge_summary is for a table with several rows for each row of the data. It summarizes them as group_rows does: by default, with the mean of each column of numbers and booleans (the mean of a boolean is the share that are true). count names a column for the number of rows:

name,court,began,ended,party,woman
Lynch,First Circuit,1995,,-1,True
Selya,First Circuit,1986,2021,1,False
Boudin,First Circuit,1992,2021,1,False
Barron,First Circuit,2014,,-1,False
Kozinski,Ninth Circuit,1985,2017,1,False
Reinhardt,Ninth Circuit,1980,2018,-1,False

amos.mergers.MergeSummary().apply(
    merged, source = "data/judges.csv", on = "court", ignorecase = True,
    count = "judges", prefix = "bench_")
print(merged.data["bench_judges"].tolist(), merged.data["bench_woman"].tolist())
# [4.0, 2.0, 4.0, nan] [0.25, 0.0, 0.25, nan]

docs.title: Reshaping data
docs.text:
Shapers change what a row is: they rearrange the same data so that each row stands for something else. Each has an opposite (the technique catalog lists them):

Shaper What it does Its parameters wide_to_long Stacks columns into rows: a row for each state, with a column for each year, becomes a row for each state in each year. columns (with name and value), or stubs (with name and separator) long_to_wide Spreads the rows of each group into columns, which is the opposite. names, values or stubs, ids, and separator lists_to_rows Makes a row for each item of a list: a row for each case becomes a row for each judge on each case. column, separator, name, and position group_rows Makes one row for each group of rows, with summaries of its columns, which is the opposite. by, how, and count

The rows of reshaped data are not the rows that it began with, so:

  • The rows get new index labels (0, 1, 2, and so on). When rows are repeated, an index with a name is kept as a column of that name.
  • A shaper must come before the data is split, so shapers belong in the wrangler.
  • The label and groups must still be columns afterward. If they are not, set the shaper's "label" and "groups" (and "task") parameters to those of the reshaped data, as for a loader.

wide_to_long stacks the columns that it is given into a value column, with a name column that says which column each value came from. With stubs, it stacks sets of columns that begin with the same names, as panel data often has: each stub becomes a column, and name has the rest of each name. long_to_wide does the opposite, with one column of values (whose new columns are named for the names alone) or one or more stubs:

states = pd.DataFrame({
    "state": ["Kansas", "Missouri"],
    "income_2019": [51, 48],
    "income_2020": [52, 49],
    "tax_2019": [0.05, 0.04],
    "tax_2020": [0.05, 0.05],
})
long = amos.shapers.WideToLong().apply(
    states, stubs = ["income", "tax"], name = "year")
print(long.data.to_dict("list"))
# {'state': ['Kansas', 'Kansas', 'Missouri', 'Missouri'], 'year': [2019, 2020, 2019, 2020], 'income': [51, 52, 48, 49], 'tax': [0.05, 0.05, 0.04, 0.05]}
amos.shapers.LongToWide().apply(long, names = "year", stubs = ["income", "tax"])
print(list(long.data.columns))
# ['state', 'income_2019', 'income_2020', 'tax_2019', 'tax_2020']

group_rows summarizes the columns of each group with the summaries in its "how": "mean", "median", "sum", "min", "max", "std", "count", "nunique", "first", "last", "any", "all", or "list". Without one, a column that is the same throughout each group keeps its value (so a case's year stays its year), the mean is taken of other numbers and booleans, and the first value is taken of anything else. A dict gives columns their own summaries.

Together, shapers and mergers join tables whose rows are different things. Opinions name the judges of each case in one cell, and the table of judges above has a row for each court that each judge has served on. To study the panels, this project makes a row for each judge on each case, adds what is known about the judge of that name who was serving on the court that year, and groups the rows into cases again:

[general]
label = "reversed"

[files]
input_folder = "data"

[panels_project]
panels_workers = "wrangler"

[wrangler]
techniques = "lists_to_rows, merge_ranges, group_rows"

[lists_to_rows_parameters]
column = "panel"
separator = ";"
name = "judge"

[merge_ranges_parameters]
source = "judges.csv"
column = "year"
start = "began"
end = "ended"
on = ["judge", "court"]
other_on = ["name", "court"]
ignorecase = true
columns = ["party", "woman"]
prefix = "panel_"
indicator = "found"

[group_rows_parameters]
by = "case"
count = "judges"

[group_rows_parameters.how]
judge = "list"
found = "sum"

argued = pd.DataFrame({
    "case": ["a1", "a2", "a3"],
    "court": ["First Circuit", "Ninth Circuit", "First Circuit"],
    "year": [2001, 2015, 2019],
    "panel": ["LYNCH; SELYA; BOUDIN", "KOZINSKI; REINHARDT", "LYNCH; BARRON; SOUTER"],
    "reversed": [True, False, True],
})
panels = amos.Project.create("panels.toml", item = argued).result
print(panels.data["judges"].tolist(), panels.data["found"].tolist())
# [3, 2, 3] [3, 2, 2]
print(panels.data["panel_party"].round(2).tolist(), panels.data["panel_woman"].tolist())
# [0.33, 0.0, -1.0] [0.3333333333333333, 0.0, 0.5]
print(panels.data["reversed"].tolist(), panels.label, panels.task)
# [True, False, True] reversed classify
print(panels.history[1])
# {'technique': 'merge_ranges', 'source': 'judges.csv', 'rows': 8, 'matched': 7, 'created': ['panel_party', 'panel_woman', 'found']}

Justice Souter sat with the First Circuit after he retired, so no row of the table of judges matches him, and the means of the third panel leave him out. The "found" column says so, which is why an indicator is worth keeping.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A technique receives its parameters from the settings and from the workers that contain it, as in chrisjen: a technique's own parameters are overridden by those of its step, then by those of its workers, and then by any passed to Project.apply. A technique that wraps a tool passes the tool only the parameters it accepts, so a parameter set for a whole worker does not break the techniques that do not use it.

If the dataset has a seed and a tool accepts a random_state that was not set, the seed is used. Every random process in a project is reproducible.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Each genre of transformer changes the features of some kinds by default: imputers change the numeric features with missing values (mode_impute changes features of every kind), scalers and mixers change the numeric features, encoders change the categorical and text features, and selectors and reducers change the numeric and boolean features. Pass columns to choose others:

cancer = sklearn.datasets.load_breast_cancer(as_frame = True)
dataset = amos.Dataset.create(cancer, seed = 43)
amos.transformers.MinMax().apply(dataset, columns = ["mean radius"])
print(dataset.history[-1]["columns"])
# ['mean radius']
print(dataset.data["mean radius"].max())
# 1.0

The columns that a transformer makes take the place of the columns it changed, so the order of the other columns does not change. Transformers are fitted to the training rows (all rows, before the data is split) and then change every row. The fitted tool is stored in fitted:

print(type(dataset.fitted["min_max"]).__name__)
# MinMaxScaler

docs.title: Interactions
docs.text:
interactions adds the product of each pair of numeric features. Give it formulas instead, each named for the interaction it makes (as in "race = offender_race * victim_race" in its settings), and it adds only those, and keeps the columns they are made from. Categorical columns make one categorical column of their combinations, each value followed by the part of its column's name that differs from the others', which an encoder can then encode. Numbers make their product, and numbers with categorical columns make the product for each combination, as a column of its own. It learns nothing from the data, so it can come before the split:

amos.transformers.Interactions().apply(
    crimes, race = "offender_race * victim_race", age_by_race = "age * victim_race")
print(crimes.data["race"].tolist())
# ['white_offender_black_victim', 'black_offender_black_victim', 'black_offender_white_victim']
print(list(crimes.data.columns))
# ['offender_race', 'victim_race', 'age', 'race', 'age_by_race_black_victim_race', 'age_by_race_white_victim_race']

docs.title: Labels and the positive class
docs.text: Metrics, encoders, and models handle labels of any type. For a binary label, the positive class is the last of Dataset.classes (such as 1, True, or "yes"), and metrics such as precision and roc_auc are about that class. For more than two classes, precision, recall, and f1 are averaged over the classes ("macro") and roc_auc compares each class with the rest. Pass average, pos_label, or the other parameters of the scikit-learn metric to change this. Encoders that learn from the label (such as target) are given the position of each class when the classes are text.

docs.title: Hyperparameter search
docs.text:
Every model accepts these parameters:

Parameter Meaning search "grid", "random", or "optuna". Without it, lists are passed to the model as they are. cv Number of cross-validation folds. Defaults to 5. If the dataset has groups, each fold keeps the rows of every group of its first group column together. n_iter Number of combinations to try in a random or Optuna search. Defaults to 10. scoring The scikit-learn scorer to compare with, such as "roc_auc". Defaults to the model's own score.

With a search, every parameter given as a list is searched. In a random or Optuna search, a list of two numbers is a range (whole numbers are drawn from it, inclusive; other numbers are drawn from between them). An Optuna search chooses each combination to try from the results of the ones before, so it usually finds good values in fewer tries, and it searches a range that spans two or more orders of magnitude (such as a learning rate from 0.001 to 0.1) on a log scale. The search uses the training rows only, and the results of every combination are stored in tables as "{name}_search".

When rows are not independent, such as the votes of the judges of one case, give the dataset groups. A search then folds whole groups (with StratifiedGroupKFold for a classifier and GroupKFold for a regression), just as the group validators do, so that no group has rows on both sides of a fold and the search never scores a model on rows that are nearly copies of ones it learned from.

amos.splitters.Stratified().apply(dataset)
amos.models.RandomForest().apply(
    dataset, search = "random", n_estimators = [20, 60], max_depth = [2, 8],
    n_iter = 3, cv = 3)
search = dataset.tables["random_forest_search"]
print(len(search), search["param_n_estimators"].between(20, 60).all())
# 3 True
amos.models.RandomForest().apply(
    dataset, search = "optuna", n_estimators = [20, 60], max_depth = [2, 8],
    n_iter = 3, cv = 3)
print(list(dataset.tables["random_forest_search"].columns[:2]))
# ['param_max_depth', 'param_n_estimators']

docs.title: Selecting features
docs.text:
Selectors keep some of the features and remove the rest. They are usually the techniques of a step of their own (such as "select"), so an experiment can compare them. Most wrap scikit-learn's feature_selection module and, like other transformers, learn which features to keep from the training rows only:

Selector Keeps variance_threshold The features whose variance is above a threshold (0). k_best, select_percentile The k features (or the percentile of them) most related to the label, by an F test or another "score_func". select_fpr, select_fdr, select_fwe The features whose p-values pass a test at "alpha" (0.05), controlling the false positive rate, the false discovery rate, or the family-wise error rate. generic_univariate The features most related to the label, by a "mode" (one of the above) and its "param". select_from_model The features that a model finds most important. recursive_elimination The features left after removing a model's least important feature again and again. recursive_elimination_cv The number of features left by recursive_elimination that scores best in cross-validation. sequential_selection_sk The features chosen by adding (or removing) one at a time, in cross-validation. sequential_selection, exhaustive_selection The set of features that scores best in mlxtend's sequential or exhaustive search. feature_group The features that the settings list.

A selector that would keep none of the features (such as select_fwe with a small "alpha") raises an error instead.

docs.title: Searching with a model
docs.text:
The selectors that fit a model take:

Parameter Meaning estimator The model: the name of a model in the library (such as random_forest), which is built for the task, or an estimator, its class, or its import path. Defaults to a logistic regression (to classify) or a linear regression. select_from_model and the recursive selectors need a model that reports the importance of each feature (as coef_ or feature_importances_). scoring For the selectors that cross-validate: the scikit-learn scorer to compare with. Defaults to accuracy or R². cv For the selectors that cross-validate: the number of folds. Defaults to 5. As in a hyperparameter search, a fold keeps the rows of every group of the first group column together.

sequential_selection adds the feature that most improves the score, one at a time (or, with forward = false, removes them), and keeps k_features features, or by default the number of features that scored best. exhaustive_selection tries every set of min_features to max_features features (1 to 3 by default), which is slow when there are many. Both need mlxtend. They, and recursive_elimination_cv, store the score of every set (or number of features) that they tried in tables as "{name}_search", best first.

features = amos.Dataset.create(cancer, seed = 43)
amos.splitters.Stratified().apply(features)
amos.selectors.SequentialSelection().apply(
    features, k_features = 3, cv = 3,
    estimator = "sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier")
print(len(features.features))
# 3
print(sorted(features.tables["sequential_selection_search"]["size"]))
# [1, 2, 3]
ranked = amos.Dataset.create(cancer, seed = 43)
amos.splitters.Stratified().apply(ranked)
amos.selectors.RecursiveElimination().apply(
    ranked, estimator = "random_forest", n_features_to_select = 4)
print(len(ranked.features))
# 4

docs.title: Groups of features
docs.text:
To compare groups of features that you choose, name each group in a "feature_groups" section of the settings, and then name the groups as techniques. Each group keeps only the features listed for it (the label and groups are always kept), so an experiment compares them like any other techniques:

[general]
label = target
seed = 43

[cancer_project]
design = experiment
criterion = roc_auc
steps = split, scale, select, model
split_techniques = stratified
scale_techniques = standard
select_techniques = size, texture, k_best
model_techniques = logit

[feature_groups]
size = mean radius, mean perimeter, mean area
texture = mean texture, worst texture

[k_best_parameters]
k = 3

data = cancer.frame
project = amos.Project.create("groups.ini", item = data)
print(sorted(b.steps["select"] for b in project.result.branches))
# ['k_best', 'size', 'texture']
print(project.result.features)
# ['worst radius', 'worst perimeter', 'worst concave points']

A listed name that is not a feature keeps the features made from it, whose names start with it and an underscore, so a group can name a column before it is encoded ("court" keeps "court_federal" and "court_state" after one_hot). A group's name must not be the name of another technique.

To keep some features in every group, list them as always_use in the section. always_use is not a group of its own (it cannot be named as a technique): each group, including a numbered feature_group, keeps its own features and those. Other selectors, such as k_best, are not affected.

[feature_groups]
always_use = mean radius
size = mean perimeter, mean area
texture = mean texture, worst texture

To use a group without the section, pass its features as columns to feature_group (or to a numbered copy, such as feature_group2, with its own parameters section).

The groups can also be the parameters of feature_group. Then a step that names feature_group names each of its groups in its place, so an experiment compares them as branches, and always_use in those parameters is kept by each of them:

[analyst]
select_techniques = feature_group

[feature_group_parameters]
always_use = mean radius
size = mean perimeter, mean area
texture = mean texture, worst texture

docs.title: Fitting models on a GPU
docs.text:
Four models can be fitted on an NVIDIA GPU, which can be much faster for large data. To use one, set use_gpu in the "general" section of the settings:

[general]
label = target
seed = 43
use_gpu = true

use_gpu is false unless the settings set it to true, so a project is fitted on the CPU unless it asks for a GPU. (Without settings, pass use_gpu = True to Dataset or Dataset.create.) With it:

Model On the GPU Notes xgboost device = "cuda" xgboost's packages for Linux and Windows include GPU support. catboost task_type = "GPU" catboost's packages for Linux and Windows include GPU support. Its results on a GPU can vary slightly from one run to the next. lightgbm device_type = "gpu" lightgbm uses OpenCL, which its packages for Linux include (NVIDIA's driver provides the OpenCL runtime). Its packages for Windows and macOS do not, so it is fitted on the CPU there. tabpfn device = "cuda" Needs a build of PyTorch for your GPU (see below). TabPFN is only practical on a CPU for about 1,000 rows or fewer.

The same goes for the models that DoubleML's and causalml's inferers fit (named by outcome_model and treatment_model, see "Causal inference" below). Every other model (and every other technique) runs on the CPU, as it does without use_gpu. When use_gpu is true:

  • amos asks NVIDIA's driver which GPUs there are, so no other package is needed. If there is none, it warns and fits every model on the CPU, so the same settings work on a computer without a GPU.
  • A model is fitted on the first GPU. To use another, set the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable (such as CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1) before starting Python.
  • If a model cannot be fitted on the GPU (because its package was built without GPU support, the GPU is too old for it, or the GPU runs out of memory, for example), it warns and is fitted on the CPU instead.
  • An inferer's models are fitted by DoubleML or causalml, which cannot switch to the CPU partway through. So before the inferer starts, each one that can use the GPU is fitted to a few made-up rows on it, and if that fails, it warns and the inferer fits that model on the CPU. This catches a package without GPU support or a GPU too old for it, but not a GPU that runs out of memory on the full data, which raises an error (set use_gpu to false to fit them on the CPU).
  • A model's own parameters take precedence. To keep one model on the CPU, set its device in its section, such as device = cpu in [xgboost_parameters]. (An inferer builds its models with their default parameters, so to keep them on the CPU, name a model that does not use a GPU or set use_gpu to false.)
  • The history records the device of each model with its parameters (but not of an inferer's models, which warn if they are fitted on the CPU instead), and export records the GPUs (their names, compute capabilities, memory, and CUDA version) in "environment.json".

A model fitted on a GPU can give slightly different results from the same model fitted on a CPU, because the GPU adds numbers in a different order. A result is reproducible on the same kind of device, which is why the device and the GPU are recorded.

Older GPUs need care. CUDA 13 does not support GPUs older than NVIDIA's Turing generation (compute capability 7.5), such as the GeForce 10 series and the TITAN Xp (compute capability 6.1). For those, use the regular xgboost package (not xgboost-cu13), which supports compute capability 5.0 and later, and, for TabPFN, a build of PyTorch for CUDA 12.6: PyTorch's builds for CUDA 12.8 and later leave out these GPUs (and PyTorch plans to stop making builds for CUDA 12.6 after version 2.14).

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126

docs.title: Statistical inference
docs.text:
Machine learning models predict. Research usually also needs inference: which features matter, by how much, and how surely. ols and glm wrap statsmodels and store a table of coefficients with their standard errors, test statistics, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals:

diabetes = sklearn.datasets.load_diabetes(as_frame = True)
dataset = amos.Dataset.create(diabetes, seed = 43)
amos.models.OLS().apply(dataset)
table = dataset.tables["ols_coefficients"]
print(list(table.columns))
# ['coefficient', 'standard_error', 'statistic', 'p_value', 'ci_lower', 'ci_upper']
print(table.loc["bmi", "p_value"] < 0.001)
# True

glm is a logistic regression (without a penalty) for classification and a linear regression for regression. Set its "family" parameter for other generalized linear models, such as "poisson" for counts. Every model that wraps statsmodels stores the same table:

Model statsmodels Use it for ols OLS Least squares regression. wls WLS Least squares with a weight for each row (the "weights" column). glm GLM Generalized linear models of any "family". quantile_regression QuantReg A "quantile" of the label (the median by default), which outliers sway less. robust_regression RLM Regression that gives outliers less weight, by "norm" (Huber's by default). mixedlm MixedLM Regression with a random intercept for each of "groups" (such as each judge). gee GEE A glm for rows correlated within "groups", with "covariance" "independence" or "exchangeable". poisson, negative_binomial, generalized_poisson, zero_inflated_poisson Poisson, NegativeBinomial, GeneralizedPoisson, ZeroInflatedPoisson Counts: whole numbers of 0 or more, which may vary more than a Poisson's or have extra zeros. logit_sm, probit Logit, Probit Two classes. Unlike logit (scikit-learn's logistic regression), logit_sm has no penalty. binomial_bayes_mixedglm BinomialBayesMixedGLM Two classes, with a random intercept for each of "groups", fitted by variational Bayes. Its table has the mean and standard deviation of each coefficient's posterior and its 95% credible interval, and no p-values. mnlogit MNLogit Any number of classes. Each class after the first has its own coefficients, named "{feature} ({class})". ordinal_regression OrderedModel Ordered classes, as an ordered logit (or probit, with "distribution"). Its classes are ordered as the categories of an ordered categorical label, and otherwise sorted.

mixedlm, gee, and binomial_bayes_mixedglm use the dataset's first group unless "groups" names a column, and the groups and weights are not features. The predictions of mixedlm and binomial_bayes_mixedglm use the fixed effects only, so they suit groups that the model has not seen. A feature that is a combination of others (collinear) has no coefficient of its own. ols, wls, glm, quantile_regression, and robust_regression share the effect among such features, and the other models leave them out: the model's dropped_ lists them, and their rows in the table of coefficients are empty. amos classifies whole numbers with few values, so set "task" to "regress" in the "general" section for a label of counts. The rest of statsmodels' models either do not predict a label from features (such as MANOVA; PCA and Factor are below), or condition the effects of groups away so that they cannot predict new rows (such as ConditionalLogit; use fixest for fixed effects).

Two of the critic's evaluators describe the features that the model learned from (the real training rows), rather than the model, with statsmodels' PCA and Factor. pca reports the eigenvalue of each principal component and the share of the variance it explains (and stores the loadings as "pca_loadings"), which shows how many dimensions the features really have. Unlike the pca_reduce reducer, it does not change the data. factor_analysis reports the loading of each feature on a few hidden factors (by default, one for each eigenvalue of the correlations above 1, rotated by varimax), with each feature's communality and uniqueness:

features = amos.Dataset.create(cancer, seed = 43)
amos.splitters.Stratified().apply(features)
amos.evaluators.PCA().apply(features)
print(round(features.tables["pca"].loc["component_6", "cumulative"], 2))
# 0.89
amos.evaluators.FactorAnalysis().apply(features)
print(list(features.tables["factor_analysis"].columns[-3:]))
# ['factor_6', 'communality', 'uniqueness']

fixest wraps pyfixest for regressions with fixed effects (an intercept for each level of a column, such as each judge or year) and standard errors clustered by a column. The columns named by its "fixed_effects" and "cluster" parameters are usually the dataset's groups, and they are not used as features. It is a least squares regression, or a logit model for classification; set "family" to "poisson" for counts or "probit":

clinics = diabetes.frame.copy()
clinics["clinic"] = [f"c{i % 10}" for i in range(len(clinics))]
dataset = amos.Dataset(clinics, label = "target", seed = 43, groups = ["clinic"])
amos.models.Fixest().apply(dataset, fixed_effects = "clinic", cluster = "clinic")
print(list(dataset.tables["fixest_coefficients"].index[:3]))
# ['age', 'sex', 'bmi']

docs.title: Choosing techniques automatically
docs.text:
Name "auto" in place of a step's techniques, and amos chooses techniques that suit the data when the workflow reaches that step. "auto" works in a step that fills missing values, encodes, samples, models, evaluates, or plots. The kind of step is found from its name ("impute", "encode", "sample", "model", "evaluate", or "plot", and a few others such as "fill", "resample", "fit", and "draw") or, for a worker without steps, from the worker's name (such as "critic" or "artist"). In a step with another name, name the chooser yourself: auto_imputer, auto_encoder, auto_sampler, auto_model, auto_evaluator, or auto_plot. The named pipelines are built on them.

Chooser What it chooses auto_imputer Nothing if no feature has missing values. Otherwise iterative_impute for the numeric features if one misses more than 5% of its values (with at least two numeric features and no more than 10,000 rows), and median_impute if not; and mode_impute for categorical and boolean features. auto_encoder For each categorical feature: one_hot if it has 15 levels or fewer ("levels"), tfidf if it is free text, target if it has more levels and the label has two classes or is regressed, count if the label has more classes, and one_hot with at most 15 columns if category_encoders is not installed. date_parts for dates. Its parameters (such as "drop") go to the encoders. auto_evaluator scorecard; classification_report and confusion for classes; regression_table for a model with coefficients and standard errors (not after an experiment); feature_importance for a model with its own importances; permutation_importance for a scikit-learn model without a regression table; shap_importance for a model of trees; and fairness for two classes with groups. auto_sampler Nothing for a regressed label or classes that are balanced (the rarest class has at least half the rows of the most common). Otherwise random_under if the rarest class has 10,000 rows or more, smote_tomek if the classes overlap, smote if the features are numeric, and random_over if they are not (or have missing values, are mostly binary, or the rarest class has fewer than 6 rows). auto_model Rules out the models that cannot do the task or use the features, and those whose assumptions the data does not meet (such as linear when the errors are not normal or the features are collinear, poisson for overdispersed counts, or naive_bayes when the features are not normal), cross-validates the first 4 of the rest ("candidates"), and fits the simplest model whose score is within one standard error of the best. It also knows the needs of ols, logit_sm, probit (two classes), and mnlogit (three or more), which it considers only when they are in "choices". auto_plot Plots of the data before a model is fitted. After, plots of the model that suit the task and the model, such as a precision-recall curve for imbalanced classes, a Q-Q plot for a model that assumes normal errors, or partial dependence for a model that is not linear.

Each chooser adds a table to the dataset's tables, named for it, with a row for each technique it considered: whether it was chosen and why (or why not). For models, it also has each model's cross-validated score. The dataset's history records the choice and the profile of the training rows that it was based on, so a paper can report how each technique was chosen.

tumors = sklearn.datasets.load_breast_cancer(as_frame = True).frame
auto_settings = {
    "general": {"label": "target", "seed": 43},
    "cancer_project": {"cancer_workers": ["analyst", "artist"]},
    "analyst": {
        "steps": ["split", "scale", "sample", "model"],
        "split_techniques": "stratified",
        "scale_techniques": "standard",
        "sample_techniques": "auto",
        "model_techniques": "auto",
    },
    "auto_model_parameters": {
        "choices": ["naive_bayes", "logit", "random_forest", "gradient_boosting"],
    },
    "artist": {"techniques": "auto"},
}
auto_project = amos.Project.create(auto_settings, item = tumors)
auto_result = auto_project.result
print(auto_result.tables["auto_sampler"].loc["none", "reason"])
# the classes are balanced: the rarest has 60% of the rows of the most common
model_choices = auto_result.tables["auto_model"]
print(model_choices.loc["naive_bayes", "reason"])
# assumes normal features, but 73% of them are not
print(model_choices["score"].round(3).dropna().to_dict())
# {'logit': 0.967, 'random_forest': 0.955, 'gradient_boosting': 0.968}
print(model_choices.index[model_choices["chosen"]].tolist())
# ['logit']
print(list(auto_result.figures))
# ['confusion_heatmap', 'roc_curve', 'calibration_curve', 'importance_plot']

gradient_boosting scored a little better than logit, but by less than one standard error, so the simpler logit was chosen. Set "simplest" to false to choose the best score instead. The "auto_model_parameters" section holds the parameters of the "model" step's "auto" (as for any technique of a step). "choices" limits the techniques that a chooser considers (in the order to prefer them). Its other parameters ("candidates", "folds", and "metric" for auto_model, "levels" for auto_encoder, and "data" for auto_plot) are described in the API reference, and any others are passed to the techniques it chooses.

The choosers can also be applied directly, and amos.auto.profile returns what they found about the data. Here, the label is counts that vary more than a Poisson model assumes:

generator = np.random.default_rng(0)
dockets = pd.DataFrame({
    "judges": generator.integers(1, 10, 500),
    "pages": generator.normal(30, 8, 500),
})
mean = np.exp(0.2 + 0.15 * dockets["judges"] + 0.01 * dockets["pages"])
dockets["appeals"] = generator.negative_binomial(2, 2 / (2 + mean))
appeal_data = amos.Dataset(dockets, label = "appeals", task = "regress", seed = 43)
appeal_data = amos.splitters.TrainTest().apply(appeal_data)
amos.auto.AutoModel().apply(
    appeal_data, choices = ["poisson", "negative_binomial", "linear", "random_forest"])
model_table = appeal_data.tables["auto_model"]
print(model_table.index[model_table["chosen"]].tolist())
# ['negative_binomial']
print(model_table.loc["poisson", "reason"])
# assumes that the variance of the counts equals their mean, but they are overdispersed (dispersion 3.31)
print(model_table.loc["linear", "reason"])
# assumes normal errors, but they are not (skewness 1.95, excess kurtosis 5.34)
found = amos.auto.profile(appeal_data)
print(found.counts, found.overdispersed, found.normal)
# True True False

docs.title: Groups and fairness
docs.text:
Research about people often needs to know whether a model treats groups differently. Name the columns that identify groups (such as race, court, or judge) as the dataset's groups, or in the "groups" setting of the "general" section. Groups stay in the data but are not features, so transformers and models do not use them. Then:

  • The fairness metrics (demographic_parity, equalized_odds, and equal_opportunity, with a "_ratio" version of each) compare the model's predictions across the dataset's first group, or the column named by their "group" parameter. They wrap fairlearn and need a label with two classes.
  • fairness makes a table of the count, selection rate, accuracy, and true and false positive rates of each group, with the largest difference and smallest ratio between groups.
  • The scorecard adds demographic_parity and equalized_odds for every branch.
  • fixest can use groups as fixed effects and clusters, and group_split keeps each row of the dataset's first group in the same set.
data = cancer.frame.copy()
data["clinic"] = np.where(np.arange(len(data)) % 3 == 0, "north", "south")
dataset = amos.Dataset(data, label = "target", seed = 43, groups = ["clinic"])
print("clinic" in dataset.features)
# False
amos.splitters.Stratified().apply(dataset)
amos.transformers.Standard().apply(dataset)
amos.models.Logit().apply(dataset)
amos.evaluators.Fairness().apply(dataset)
print(list(dataset.tables["fairness"].index))
# ['north', 'south', 'difference', 'ratio']
print(0 <= amos.metrics.EqualizedOdds().measure(dataset) <= 1)
# True

Rows that a sampler copies keep their groups. Synthetic rows (made by smote, for example) have no groups.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text:
conformal turns any model's predictions into intervals (for regression) or sets of classes (for classification) that contain the true value for at least a chosen share of rows, with MAPIE's cross-conformal methods. The share of test rows covered and the width of the intervals (or the size of the sets) are stored in metrics:

dataset = amos.Dataset.create(diabetes, seed = 43)
amos.splitters.TrainTest().apply(dataset)
amos.models.Linear().apply(dataset)
amos.evaluators.Conformal().apply(dataset, confidence = 0.9)
print(list(dataset.tables["conformal"].columns))
# ['actual', 'prediction', 'lower', 'upper', 'covered']
print(dataset.metrics["coverage"] > 0.8)
# True

docs.title: Causal inference
docs.text:
A model predicts the label. An inferer measures how much a treatment (such as a program or a ruling) changes the label, after accounting for the other features, or, for a time series, which variables cause which others and when.
