docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

• Requires bobbie 0.3.3 or later, so an ini list can go on over several lines and the rest of a line after a # with spaces on both sides is a comment.
  • The label can be a column that the wrangler makes (such as with derive_columns). Until then it is pending: Dataset keeps its name rather than raising a KeyError, infers the task once the column is made, and raises an error if the label is used before. The new Dataset.has_label says whether the label is a column yet.
  • Added set_kinds, a munger that gives each column a kind ("dummy", "categorical", or "numerical") in the smallest type that holds it exactly (int8 for dummies, the "category" type, and the smallest integer or float type for numbers), and infers the kinds of the columns it is not given. A dummy with missing values raises an error, and a classified label of booleans becomes a dummy. The kinds are kept in the new Dataset.kinds, so a dummy is one of the dataset's booleans.
  • rename_columns, filter_rows, and derive_columns take settings named for columns, so they need no mappings in an ini file (state = state_abbreviation, state = not in ['GU', 'PR'], and minor = victim_age < 18). A condition of filter_rows can start with a comparison, "not" and a value, or be a value or list.
  • Words that are not columns in the conditions of filter_rows and the expressions of derive_columns are values, so text needs no quotes (offender_race == B). A word that is both a column and a value of the column it is compared to raises an error.
  • map_values without "values" uses the map or function registered for each of its columns with the new amos.register_value_map.
  • frequencies takes columns = all, which counts the categorical and boolean features, including the dummies of set_kinds.
  • interactions takes formulas, such as race = offender_race * victim_race. Categorical columns make one categorical column of their combinations (such as "white_offender_black_victim"), numbers make their product, and both make the product for each combination.
  • Groups of features can be the parameters of feature_group (such as raw = a, b in "feature_group_parameters"). A step that names feature_group then names each group in its place, so an experiment compares them as branches, and always_use in those parameters is kept by each group.
  • Features listed as always_use in the "feature_groups" section of the settings are kept by every feature group (including a numbered feature_group with its own "columns"), so they are in every group's path. always_use is not a technique of its own, and other selectors are not affected.
  • Metrics are no longer steps of a workflow. Metric is now a chrisjen.Criteria rather than an Operation, so it has no apply and is stored under "criteria" in the library instead of with the techniques. Name a metric as a worker's criterion, or in the metrics of a scorecard or validator; listing one among a worker's techniques raises a TypeError that says so. In Python, call measure for a score (it now uses the metric's own parameters, which a keyword argument overrides).

• Added selectors, a new genre of analyst techniques that keep some of the features and remove the rest (the new selectors module and Selector class), usually in a step of their own such as "select". k_best, select_percentile, variance_threshold, sequential_selection, and exhaustive_selection moved there from the reducers (their names in settings are unchanged, but their classes are now in amos.selectors, and the Reducer genre has only pca_reduce). New selectors wrap the rest of scikit-learn's feature_selection module: select_fpr, select_fdr, select_fwe, generic_univariate, select_from_model, recursive_elimination, recursive_elimination_cv (which adds a "{name}_search" table of the score of each number of features), and sequential_selection_sk (which needs no optional package). The selectors that fit a model take the name of a model in the library as their "estimator" (such as random_forest, which is built for the task), and a selector that would keep no features raises an error.
  • Added feature groups: each group named in a new "feature_groups" section of the settings (such as demographics = age, sex, race) is a technique that keeps only its features, so an experiment can compare groups of features that you chose (select_techniques = demographics, case_facts). A listed column that has been encoded keeps the columns made from it (so "court" keeps "court_federal" and "court_state" after one_hot). The feature_group technique does the same with the features passed as its "columns".
  • The scorecard of a dataset that did not come from an experiment lists its selectors as a step, including feature groups that are only in a project's own library (a technique that is not in chrisjen.library is listed under the "genre" in its history entry, if it has one).
  • Requires chrisjen 0.4.2, camina 0.2.4, and nagata 0.2.1 or later, and the lock file uses the latest chrisjen, camina, nagata, bobbie, bunches, holden, miller, and wonka. All of them ship the py.typed marker, so the mypy override that followed their untyped imports is gone.
  • The parameters of techniques (base.GenericDict) have str keys, as chrisjen now types them, and the casts of Loader.build and Merger.build are gone, since chrisjen's build returns the class it is called on.
  • The axes of plots start at 0 (or end at 0, for negative numbers), unless they show something with no natural zero (the values of the features, the label of a regression or the model's predictions of it, or the parameters of a model in search_plot and validation_curve), or are axes of names, dates, a logarithmic scale, or a heatmap. The new "start_at_zero" parameter of every plot ("x", "y", "xy", or "") picks the axes (anything else raises a ValueError).
  • The panels of a plot that measure the same thing share their ranges: the counts of histograms and count_plots, the scores of search_plot, and the contributions of shape_functions. In a pair_plot, each feature has one range, on the x axes of its column and the y axes of its row.
  • The lock file uses category-encoders 2.11.2, coverage 7.17.0, fairlearn 0.15.0, great-tables 1.1.0, mapie 1.6.0, markdown-exec 1.12.6, mkdocs-coverage 2.0.1, mkdocs-material 9.8.0, pandas 3.1.0, polars 2.1.0, pre-commit 4.7.0, pyarrow 26.0.0, ruff 0.17.3, statsmodels 0.15.0, and uv 0.13.6, and the workflows use astral-sh/setup-uv 10.3.2.

• Added Clerk (in the new clerks module), a nagata.FileManager that is now the clerk of every Project and loader. It keeps data and results outside a project's code, in the "workspace" that holds the "code" folder: data in its "data" folder (or in a subfolder of it named by the new "data_subfolder" setting of the "files" section, such as "crime/nibrs"), and each run's results in its "studies" folder. The workspace is the folder that holds the nearest "code" folder above the current folder (or the current folder, if there is none), unless the AMOS_WORKSPACE environment variable or options._DEFAULT_ROOT names another. Before, a project kept its files in the current folder, so a project that relied on that should set "root_folder", "input_folder", or "output_folder" in its "files" section.

• Added named pipelines (the new pipelines module and Pipeline class). pipeline = classification in the "general" section (or the project's section) fills in the settings of the analyst, critic, and artist, so a study can be a label, a seed, and a pipeline. The pipelines are classification, regression, and count_regression, which compare models in an experiment, and classification_inference, regression_inference, count_inference, panel_classification, and panel_regression, which fit one model for its coefficients (without scaling or resampling, and with each category encoded against a reference level). Settings that you write win over the pipeline's, a worker's own section can name a pipeline for that worker, the pipeline sets "task" if it is not set, and the filled-in settings are in Project.idea and the exported "settings.json". Add a Pipeline to pipelines.PIPELINES to name your own.
  • Added three choosers, which the pipelines use and "auto" now resolves to in steps named "impute", "encode", and "evaluate" (and in a worker named "critic"): auto_imputer fills missing values (with iterative_impute when many numeric values are missing, median_impute otherwise, and mode_impute for categories); auto_encoder encodes each categorical feature by its number of levels (one_hot for 15 or fewer, target for more with a label of two classes or a regressed one, count for a label of more classes, tfidf for free text, and date_parts for dates); and auto_evaluator applies the evaluators that suit the task and the model.
  • auto_model knows the needs of ols, logit_sm, probit, and mnlogit (such as the number of classes), which it considers when they are named in "choices".
  • Fixed smote_tomek and smote_enn marking every training row as synthetic, because they remove some of the original rows after adding rows. Validators then had no real rows to cross-validate, and choosers profiled none. Each row they keep that equals an original row is now real.
  • Fixed fixest predicting missing values (and so a scorecard failing with "Input contains NaN") for rows whose level of a fixed effect has no estimate: a level that was not in the training rows, or one that pyfixest dropped (a singleton, or a level separated by having rows of only one class). Such a row is now predicted with that fixed effect at the average of its estimated levels. The estimates of the levels are in the model's effect_levels_. A fixest model can therefore be validated by group_k_fold (each held-out group is predicted with the average fixed effect), which used to fail with "could not predict".
  • Fixed permutation_importance, shap_partial_dependence, and decision_regions failing for a model that needs columns besides its features, such as the fixed effects and cluster of a fixest model. permutation_importance and shap_partial_dependence hold those columns at each row's own values (as shap_importance does), and decision_regions holds them at their most common values in the real training rows (as it holds the other features at their medians). permutation_importance also works for models that are not scikit-learn estimators, which scikit-learn's scorers rejected.
  • Fixed the report of a project saying that an experiment that conserves memory chose "the best of 1 paths". It now gives the number of paths compared.
  • Inferers (such as dr_learner and partially_linear) now leave out the rows that a sampler (such as random_over or smote) added to the training rows, which counted some rows more than once and biased the estimates and their standard errors. The data is put back afterwards.

• Added a conserve_memory setting (from chrisjen's new option for comparing workers), for an experiment's section or for every experiment in the "general" section. An experiment that conserves memory scores each combination as soon as it is tried and keeps only the best whole dataset so far, rather than every combination's dataset until the last one is done, which ran out of memory with many combinations of a large dataset. Its comparison table, scores, and branches are the same, but only the winner's branch has its whole dataset, so a regression_table has only the winner's model. Experiment.outcomes has the outcome of each combination (its label and group columns, predictions, probabilities, and metrics). Requires chrisjen 0.4.0 or later.

• A validator resamples only the model's features when it applies the analysis's samplers to each fold, and gives each copied row the other columns that the model needs (such as the fixed effects and cluster of a fixest model) from the row it copies, as a sampler does for the groups. Before, smote and the other samplers that interpolate numbers failed in a validator of a fixest model whose fixed effects were text.
  • shap_importance (and the SHAP plots, which use it) explains a model that needs columns besides its features, such as a fixest model, by explaining each row with those columns held at its own values, so its SHAP values are the effects of its features given its fixed effects. Before, it failed because the explained rows had no fixed effects.
  • feature_importance (and importance_plot) leaves out the features that a model dropped, such as the collinear features that pyfixest drops, rather than failing because there were fewer coefficients than features.

• regression_table takes "sets" of features (such as the dummy variables of one category, as "family, partner, stranger; under_12, teen" in settings), whose members' average marginal effects are each the change from the set's reference (every member 0) to that member alone, rather than from moving each dummy on its own, which made rows that cannot happen.
  • Added techniques that wrap mlxtend, which the new mlxtend extra (and all) installs: sequential_selection and exhaustive_selection, reducers that search for the set of features with which a model (a logistic or linear regression, or "estimator") scores best in cross-validation, folding by the dataset's first group as a model's search does, and store the score of each set as "{name}_search"; association_rules, a describer of which values (of the categorical and boolean columns, and of a classified label) tend to appear in the same rows; bias_variance, an evaluator that splits the model's expected loss on the test rows into its bias and variance; and decision_regions, a plot of the class that a classifier predicts across two features.
  • Added dtreeviz's plots of decision trees, which the explain extra now installs: tree_leaf_sizes, tree_leaf_distributions, tree_leaf_purity, tree_feature_space, and tree_prediction_path. They draw a decision_tree or one tree of a random_forest, extra_trees, or adaboost model (and tree_leaf_sizes and tree_leaf_distributions one tree of an xgboost or lightgbm model), in the style of the other figures. dtreeviz's drawing of a whole tree is not wrapped, since it needs Graphviz and makes only SVG files; tree_plot draws one.
  • models.search_folds returns the folds of a hyperparameter search (which Model._folds now calls), so that other techniques can fold by groups as a search does.
  • Plots that draw with matplotlib.pyplot (shap's, and now mlxtend's and dtreeviz's) are lent their figure by plots._lent, which also keeps pyplot.show from opening a window while they draw.
  • A model's hyperparameter search ("grid", "random", or "optuna") keeps the rows of each group of the dataset's first group column in one fold, as the group validators do, when the dataset has groups: with StratifiedGroupKFold for a classifier and GroupKFold for a regression. Before, its folds divided the rows at random, so rows of one group (such as the votes of the judges of one case) could be on both sides of a fold and the search scored a model on rows it had partly seen. A row with a missing group is a group of its own.
  • Brought in the CI fixes of snickerdoodle 0.4.3: GitHub releases are made with the GitHub CLI (in place of the deprecated gh-action-auto-release Action), with the released version's section of CHANGELOG.md as their notes, only from main and after the tests and linters pass. The test matrix now runs every Python version it names, instead of recreating the environment with Python 3.11 at uv run.

• A technique now writes apply instead of implement, following chrisjen 0.3.0 (now the oldest version that amos accepts), whose nodes all do. Calling apply works as before: it accepts anything that Dataset.create accepts, fills in the technique's parameters, and records the technique in the dataset's history. That work moved to Operation._call_apply, which chrisjen calls around each apply (but not around a super().apply call from a subclass). A technique that wrote implement must rename it to apply.
  • Added the auto module, which lets a step's techniques be "auto" in the settings: amos then chooses techniques that suit the data when the workflow reaches the step. "auto" works in a step that samples, models, or plots (found from the name of the step, or of a worker such as "artist"), and auto_sampler, auto_model, and auto_plot can be named in any step. auto_sampler resamples only imbalanced classes, with a sampler that suits their size, overlap, and features. auto_model rules out the models that cannot use the features or whose assumptions the data does not meet (normal errors, collinear features, the dispersion of counts, and so on), cross-validates the rest, and fits the simplest model within one standard error of the best. auto_plot draws the data before a model is fitted, and the plots that suit the task and the model after. Each records a table of the techniques it considered and why each was or was not chosen, and amos.auto.profile returns what it found about the data.
  • Fixed validators, conformal, explain_weights, feature_importance, and the marginal effects of regression_table for lightgbm models whose feature names have spaces. lightgbm replaces the spaces with underscores, so the names it reports were not columns of the data: validators failed, and the other techniques named features that the data did not have (and regression_table left them out). utilities.feature_names now gives back the columns that a model was fitted to.
  • lightgbm is now quiet, as its default "verbose" of -1 meant it to be. The setting never reached lightgbm, which takes it only through **kwargs, so lightgbm printed a warning for each tree it could not split further. A model's keyword_parameters now names such parameters.
  • Added the regression_table evaluator, which reports every model the way Stata, R, and statsmodels report regressions: a column for each branch of the experiment (or for the final model), each feature's estimate with stars and its standard error in parentheses, and the kind of estimates, the number of observations, and cross-validated metrics below them. A model that reports its coefficients (the statsmodels and pyfixest models) shows them. Any other model shows each feature's average marginal effect, with standard errors from refitting the model to bootstrap samples of the training rows ("simulations", 100 by default). Set "marginal" to true to show marginal effects for every model. RegressionTable.create makes one from a dataset, an applied project, or several datasets, and it is saved in the same formats as a scorecard. Word documents, images, and to_text look like Stata's output of regress (a block for each model, with its statistics above a table of "Coef." or "dy/dx", "Std. Err.", "t" or "z", the p-value, and the 95% confidence interval), and csv, Markdown, LaTeX, and HTML put the models side by side. Set "style" to "columns" to put them side by side in Word documents and images too. Project.export saves each regression table in the workflow. The README shows the tables of the best logit and xgboost branches of its study.
  • Each Branch of an experiment now keeps a weak reference to the whole dataset that it made (Branch.dataset), so the fitted model of every branch can be reached after the experiment. Copies and pickles of a branch do not keep it.

  • The scorecard's exports are now shared with the regression table. LaTeX tables now escape "<" and ">".

  • A path to a data file passed as a project's item, or to Dataset.create, is now read with nagata's formats, just as load_file reads it, so it may be in any format that nagata knows (such as json lines, fixed-width, HDF, ORC, XML, or SAS) or compressed (such as "cases.csv.gz"). A project reads it with its clerk. Before, it was read with amos's own list of 11 pandas readers. A format added to nagata (a subclass of nagata.base.FileFormat) is now read by an item too.

  • The error for a file whose format is not known from its name now lists the extensions that nagata knows.

• Added the use_gpu setting to the "general" section, which fits the models that can use a GPU (xgboost, catboost, lightgbm, and tabpfn) on an NVIDIA GPU. It is false unless the settings set it to true, and it is kept in the new Dataset.use_gpu. amos finds GPUs by asking NVIDIA's driver, so it needs no other package. If there is no GPU, or a model cannot be fitted on it, the model warns and is fitted on the CPU. export records the GPUs in "environment.json".
  • DoubleML's and causalml's inferers fit their outcome_model and treatment_model on the GPU too when use_gpu is true. Those packages fit the models themselves, so each model that can use a GPU is first fitted to a few rows on it, and if that fails, it warns and the inferer fits that model on the CPU.
  • tabpfn is now fitted on the CPU unless use_gpu is true, as a model or as an inferer's model. Before, it used a GPU whenever PyTorch found one.
  • Models now record their device in their history's parameters (such as xgboost's "device" or catboost's "task_type").

• Fixed the stratified and train_test splitters failing ("only integer scalar arrays can be converted to a scalar index") when the index of the data was text and pyarrow was installed. pandas stores text with pyarrow when it is installed, and scikit-learn cannot select rows from an index that is stored that way. The splitters now give scikit-learn the positions of the rows to divide, as group_split already did, and look up their index labels afterward. Every split has the same rows as before.
  • Added a CITATION.cff file and a citation section to the README
  • Changed the development status to Beta
  • Made the README badges larger

• Updated to the snickerdoodle 0.4.0 template
  • Made ruff prefer single quotes
  • Made ruff ignore boolean default positional arguments (FBT002)
  • Excluded uv.lock from the large file check

• Added mergers, a new genre for the wrangler, for data from tables that are not organized the same way. A merger matches each row of the data to a row of another table (its "source": a data file, which is loaded with the project's clerk, or a table) and adds that row's columns. merge_keys matches the row with the same keys, merge_nearest the row with the nearest date or number, and merge_ranges the row whose range has a date or number in it. merge_summary adds summaries of every row with the same keys. A merger never adds, removes, or reorders rows, and records how many rows it matched in the dataset's history. Every merger takes "columns", "prefix", and "indicator".
  • Added shapers, a new genre for the wrangler, which change what a row is. wide_to_long stacks columns into rows and long_to_wide spreads rows into columns, with "stubs" for sets of columns such as "income_2019" and "income_2020". lists_to_rows makes a row for each item of a list (such as each judge of a case), and group_rows makes one row for each group of rows, with summaries of its columns. A shaper comes before the data is split, and takes "label", "task", and "groups" for the reshaped data.
  • In Python, the genres are amos.Merger (whose subclasses write match) and amos.Shaper (whose subclasses write shape), in amos.mergers and amos.shapers. The advanced user guide has new sections on merging and reshaping data.
  • Fixed Project.export failing ("keys must be str, int, float, bool or None") when the dataset's history had keys that a json file cannot store. A sampler recorded the number of rows of each class by numpy values when the label was pandas booleans that allow missing values (the "boolean" type). Samplers now record the classes as plain Python values, and export saves any other such key as its plain value or its str, as it already saved values.

• Renamed effects to inferers and moved them from the analyst to the critic, since they judge what the data can say about causes. In Python, amos.effects is now amos.inferers and amos.Effect is now amos.Inferer, and the genre is "inferer" in the library. The names of partially_linear and interactive_regression in settings are unchanged. The inferers of each package are a genre of their own (Doubleml, Dowhy, Causalml, and Tigramite).
  • Added the rest of DoubleML's models: partially_linear_iv, partially_logistic, partially_linear_panel, interactive_iv, potential_outcomes, quantile_effects, difference_in_differences, regression_discontinuity, and sample_selection. difference_in_differences handles two or more periods, units first treated in different periods, panels (with "unit"), and repeated cross-sections, and stores the effect by the number of periods since the treatment as "{name}_periods". regression_discontinuity is sharp or fuzzy, as the data show, and needs rdrobust.
  • Added DoWhy's estimators: regression_adjustment, glm_adjustment, doubly_robust, propensity_matching, propensity_stratification, propensity_weighting, distance_matching, and instrumental_variable, with bootstrapped confidence intervals ("simulations") and DoWhy's refuters ("refuters"), whose results are stored as "{name}_refutations".
  • Added causalml's meta-learners: s_learner, t_learner, x_learner, dr_learner, and tmle, which compare each value of the treatment with a "control" and store the effect for each row as "{name}_effects". causalml's R-learner, causal forest, and doubly robust learner with an instrument are left out, since they do not work in causalml 0.17.
  • Added tigramite's causal discovery in time series: pcmci, pcmci_plus, and lpcmci, which store the causal links between the variables that they find, and time_series_effect, which estimates the effect of one series on the label at a lag.
  • The causal extra installs DoubleML, tigramite, rdrobust, and networkx, and causalml on Python 3.11 and 3.12 or DoWhy on Python 3.13 and later. causalml has no version for Python 3.13 and later, and on Python 3.11 and 3.12 the versions of DoWhy that work with pandas 3 cannot be installed with it. causalml's and DoWhy's inferers explain where they cannot be used.
  • Every class and function that wraps a tool from another package names the tool and its package in a "Wraps:" section of its docstring, with a link to its documentation, so the API reference shows which tool each technique uses.
  • Using causalml no longer changes matplotlib's style (causalml sets it to "fivethirtyeight" when its meta-learners are imported).
  • The advanced user guide's section on causal inference covers every inferer, with a table of which to use for each design of study.

• Renamed scikit-learn's logistic regression from sk_logit to logit (amos.models.Logit), and statsmodels' logistic regression from logit to logit_sm (amos.models.LogitSM), whose table of coefficients is now "logit_sm_coefficients". Settings that name sk_logit must use logit, and settings that name logit for statsmodels' model must use logit_sm.
  • Added mungers, a new genre for the wrangler. A munger changes what is in columns, or makes new columns from them, without adding or removing rows, a whole column at a time with the vectorized methods of pandas. auto_categorize, convert_types, and strip_text moved to the mungers from the cleaners (in Python, they are now in amos.mungers; their names in settings are unchanged). The new mungers are flag_patterns, count_patterns, map_patterns, extract_pattern, extract_all, split_text, replace_text, normalize_text, parse_numbers, parse_dates, parse_booleans, map_values, coalesce, combine_flags, and derive_columns. A munger records the columns that it changed and created in the dataset's history.
  • Figures share one style. By default, it is SciencePlots' "science" and "nature" styles (one column of Nature, 3.3 inches wide, with 7-point text) and its "bright" color cycle, which people with color blindness can tell apart. Every plot takes "style" (which can be "xkcd"), "colors", and "latex" (off unless asked for, although "science" turns LaTeX on). The defaults are options._PLOT_STYLE and options._PLOT_COLORS, and SciencePlots is in the plots extra.
  • A plot's usual size is scaled to the width of its style. The SHAP plots and influence_plot, whose packages fix the sizes of their text, keep their usual sizes, and the style's text is enlarged to match.
  • Project.export saves figures at 300 dots per inch (options._FIGURE_DPI).
  • shap_bar and shap_waterfall use the first two colors of the style's cycle, shap_waterfall writes each value beside its arrow, and both no longer fail with styles that show minor ticks. The plots that scikit-learn and statsmodels draw (actual_vs_predicted, residual_plot, qq_plot, and partial_dependence) use the colors of the style's cycle, and axes of categories and heatmaps have no minor ticks.
  • The README's study adds xgboost and draws a confusion heatmap and a SHAP waterfall. The advanced user guide has new sections on munging data and the styles of figures.

• Renamed scikit-learn's logistic regression from logit to sk_logit, and the scikit-learn PCA reducer from pca to pca_reduce, so that logit and pca are the statsmodels techniques below. Settings that name logit or pca must use the new names to keep their old behavior.
  • Replaced lifelines with statsmodels for the survival tools (cox, kaplan_meier, concordance, and survival_curves), so the survival extra installs statsmodels. amos now requires pandas 3.
  • Added loaders, a new genre for the wrangler: load_file, download, and openml load data through the project's clerk (its nagata.FileManager). Files are found, and downloads are saved, in the clerk's input folder, and a project with a loader needs no item. Loaders read every row and read text as UTF-8.
  • Added validators, a new genre for the analyst: k_fold, stratified_k_fold, group_k_fold, stratified_group_k_fold, repeated_k_fold, repeated_stratified_k_fold, shuffle_split, stratified_shuffle_split, group_shuffle_split, leave_one_group_out, leave_one_row_out, and time_series_split. After the model, a validator refits copies of it on folds of the training rows and scores each fold with the critic's metrics. Their means are stored in metrics as "cv_{metric}", so scorecards and an experiment's comparison show them.
  • Datasets record the training rows that a sampler made up (synthetic). Validators never score them, and apply the samplers again in each fold.
  • Added models from statsmodels, each with a table of coefficients: logit, probit, mnlogit, ordinal_regression, wls, quantile_regression, robust_regression, mixedlm, gee, binomial_bayes_mixedglm, poisson, negative_binomial, generalized_poisson, and zero_inflated_poisson. mixedlm, gee, and binomial_bayes_mixedglm use the dataset's first group unless "groups" names a column.
  • The statsmodels models that cannot estimate a feature that is a combination of others (collinear) leave it out, the same way on every computer: the model's dropped_ lists it, and its row in the table of coefficients is empty.
  • A glm or gee of a family that regresses refuses a classified label, and the models of counts explain how to regress a label of few whole numbers. Effects can use the statsmodels models as learners.
  • Added pca and factor_analysis to the critic: statsmodels' analyses of the features that the model learned from.
  • influence_plot now draws a glm.
  • The README's table of stages lists every technique, divided into the steps of each stage, with a link to each one's API documentation. The advanced user guide has new sections on loading data and cross-validation.

• Added eleven plots from shap to the artist: shap_bar, shap_beeswarm, shap_violin, shap_heatmap, shap_decision, shap_embedding, shap_waterfall, shap_force, shap_scatter (a dependence plot), shap_partial_dependence, and shap_group_difference. They draw the SHAP values that shap_importance found (or find them), for the class chosen with "category" (by default, the last class). shap draws with matplotlib.pyplot, so these plots lend it their figure while it draws, without opening a window, and leave pyplot as it was. The random numbers that shap uses to jitter dots and to bootstrap are seeded with the dataset's seed, so the figures are reproducible.
  • Added plots from the other packages:
  • scikit-learn: calibration_curve, det_curve, partial_dependence, learning_curve, validation_curve, and tree_plot.
  • seaborn: box_plots, count_plots, pair_plot, label_plot, and missing_heatmap, split or colored by the label's classes (or by a group, or by "by").
  • statsmodels: qq_plot and influence_plot.
  • InterpretML: shape_functions, the shape functions of an explainable_boosting model.
  • Plots of the tables made with other packages: coefficient_plot (of the coefficients of ols, glm, fixest, or cox, or of an effect from DoubleML), fairness_plot (fairlearn), prediction_intervals (MAPIE), and search_plot (of any search, including Optuna's).
  • survival_curves can add a table of the number of rows at risk (at_risk).
  • A plot can have its own usual size (Plot.size), which "width" and "height" still change, and a plot whose tool makes its own figure (as shap's force plot does) can return that figure from draw.
  • Moved the technique catalog out of the advanced user guide into its own page of the user guide, "Technique Catalog". Its tables are written from the techniques' docstrings by docs/scripts/technique_catalog.py, and a test checks that they are up to date.

• Replaced the scorecard technique of the critic stage with Scorecard, which compares every branch of an analysis: one row for each combination of techniques that the most recent experiment tried, ranked by its criterion, with the technique used at each step and every standard metric for the task, computed from each branch's own predictions. It still stores the final model's scores in the dataset's metrics. Its table now has one row for each branch (instead of one row for each metric).
  • A scorecard can be saved as a csv file (to_csv), a Markdown table (to_markdown), a Word document (to_word), or an image (to_image), or in all four formats at once (export). Scorecard.create makes one from a dataset or an applied project, and Project.scorecard returns the project's scorecard. Project.export saves it in every format.
  • An experiment now keeps a Branch (the technique used at each step, the score, and the predictions) for every combination in the winning dataset's branches.
  • Added the word extra, which installs python-docx for Word documents.
  • Added the scorecard of the README's breast cancer study to the README.
  • Added groups to Dataset (and a "groups" setting in the "general" section): columns that identify groups of people or places, which stay in the data but are not features. Cleaners and samplers keep them (synthetic rows have none), and group_split uses the first group by default.
  • Added support for 13 more packages, for 139 techniques in ten genres:
  • fairlearn: six fairness metrics (demographic_parity, equalized_odds, and equal_opportunity, with a "_ratio" version of each) in the new GroupMetric genre, and the fairness evaluator, which compares the model across groups. The scorecard adds demographic_parity and equalized_odds for every branch when a dataset has groups and a label with two classes.

  • Mapie

    the conformal evaluator, which makes prediction intervals (or sets of classes) with a known rate of coverage.

  • eli5: the explain_weights evaluator.
  • InterpretML: the explainable_boosting model, whose term importances feature_importance reports.
  • CatBoost: the catboost model, which uses categorical columns directly.
  • TabPFN: the tabpfn model (in its own tabpfn extra, which is not part of all because it needs PyTorch).
  • pyfixest: the fixest model, a regression (or logit) with fixed effects and clustered standard errors, whose coefficients are stored in a table.
  • lifelines: the cox model, the concordance metric, the kaplan_meier describer, and the survival_curves plot.
  • DoubleML: the new Effect genre, with partially_linear and interactive_regression, which estimate the causal effect of a treatment with double machine learning.
  • skrub: the date_parts, gap, min_hash, and tfidf encoders.
  • Optuna: search = "optuna" for any model.
  • Polars: Dataset.create accepts Polars data frames (lazy or not).
  • great_tables: scorecards as HTML tables (to_html). Scorecards can also be saved as LaTeX tables (to_latex), and export saves both.
  • Added the causal, fairness, polars, survival, tables, tuning, uncertainty, and tabpfn extras, and added packages to the boosting, encoders, explain, and statistics extras.
  • Added Dataset.dates, the names of the date and time columns.
  • Code that calls pyfixest no longer changes the level or handlers of the root logger.
  • Added recipes for fairness and for fixed effects, and sections of the advanced user guide on groups and fairness, uncertainty, causal effects, and survival analysis.
  • Left private classes, methods, and functions out of the API documentation.

• Rebuilt amos as Automated Modeling for Open Scholarship: a package for reproducible data science in academic research, built on chrisjen 0.2.0. A study is described in a settings file (or a dict), which chrisjen turns into a workflow of workers, steps, and techniques.
  • Added Dataset, the item that flows through an amos workflow. It keeps the data in one pandas.DataFrame with the label, the training and test rows, the fitted model, its predictions and probabilities, metrics, tables, figures, fitted tools, and a history of every technique applied.
  • Added Operation, the base class of every amos technique, and 116 techniques in nine genres, each stored in the chrisjen library under its snake case name: cleaners (10), describers (6), splitters (4), transformers (imputers, scalers, encoders, mixers, and reducers: 37), samplers (9), models (19), metrics (17), evaluators (6), and plots (8). They wrap scikit-learn, category_encoders, imbalanced-learn, xgboost, lightgbm, statsmodels, shap, matplotlib, and seaborn. Optional packages are imported only when they are used, and are installed with extras (such as amos[all]).
  • Transformers and samplers learn from the training rows only, keep named columns, can be limited to some columns, and are given the label when they are fitted. Models do both tasks where they can, search for the best hyperparameters when asked, and (with ols and glm) report coefficients with standard errors, p-values, and confidence intervals. Every metric is also a chrisjen.Criteria, so it can be an experiment's criterion.
  • Added the Experiment design, which tries every combination of techniques, keeps the best, and adds a table comparing every combination.
  • Added amos.Project, which makes data into a Dataset, reads "label", "task", and "seed" from the "general" section of the settings, applies the workflow to a copy of the data, passes the seed to every tool that takes a random_state, and exports the report, settings, environment, history, predictions, tables, and figures.
  • Added the Findings report.
  • Added an ROC curve and an importance plot from the README's breast cancer study to the README, with docs/scripts/readme_figures.py to draw them again.
  • Added tests that compare amos with each package that it wraps, using the same data, parameters, and seed.
  • Removed the general-purpose containers, converters, factories, and registries of 0.1.x. They now live in bunches, camina, holden, and wonka.
  • Moved to the snickerdoodle template, based on uv and hatchling, with ruff, mypy, pre-commit, mkdocs, and GitHub Actions. The README and documentation examples are run by the unit tests.
• The last release of the earlier, general-purpose amos, a toolkit of containers and converters for Python projects.

docs.title: Our Pledge
docs.text: In the interest of fostering an open and welcoming environment, we as contributors and maintainers pledge to make participation in our project and our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

docs.title: Our Standards
docs.text:
Examples of behavior that contributes to creating a positive environment include:

  • Using welcoming and inclusive language
  • Being respectful of differing viewpoints and experiences
  • Gracefully accepting constructive criticism
  • Focusing on what is best for the community
  • Showing empathy towards other community members

Examples of unacceptable behavior by participants include:

  • The use of sexualized language or imagery and unwelcome sexual attention or advances
  • Trolling, insulting/derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
  • Public or private harassment
  • Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or electronic address, without explicit permission
  • Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

docs.title: Our Responsibilities
docs.text:
Project maintainers are responsible for clarifying the standards of acceptable behavior and are expected to take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any instances of unacceptable behavior.

Project maintainers have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, or to ban temporarily or permanently any contributor for other behaviors that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This Code of Conduct applies within all project spaces, and it also applies when an individual is representing the project or its community in public spaces. Examples of representing a project or community include using an official project e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event. Representation of a project may be further defined and clarified by project maintainers.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported by contacting any of the following people:

  • Corey Rayburn Yung (coreyrayburnyung@gmail.com)

All complaints will be reviewed and investigated and will result in a response that is deemed necessary and appropriate to the circumstances. The project team is obligated to maintain confidentiality with regard to the reporter of an incident. Further details of specific enforcement policies may be posted separately.

Project maintainers who do not follow or enforce the Code of Conduct in good faith may face temporary or permanent repercussions as determined by other members of the project's leadership.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome and greatly appreciated! Every little bit helps, and credit will always be given.

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
amos uses uv to manage its environment. After cloning the repository, install every dependency (including the optional packages that the tests use) and the pre-commit hooks:

uv sync
uv run pre-commit install

Then run the tests, the linter, and the type checker:

uv run pytest
uv run ruff check
uv run mypy

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Follow this basic process:

  1. Fork and clone the repository.
  2. Create a new branch: git checkout -b feature-or-bugfix-name.
  3. Edit the code.
  4. If you added functionality or features, update the documentation accordingly.

If you are unsure about how to fix or ignore a warning, just let the continuous integration fail, and we will help you during review.

Don't bother updating the changelog, we will take care of this.

docs.title: Adding a technique
docs.text:
Most contributions to amos are new techniques. To add one:

  1. Find the module of its genre (loaders, cleaners, mungers, mergers, shapers, describers, splitters, transformers, samplers, models, validators, metrics, evaluators, inferers, or plots) and copy a similar technique. Every class is a dataclasses.dataclass.
  2. Wrap tools from other packages by their import paths (in contents or tools), not by importing them at the top of a module. They are imported only when the technique is used, so amos stays light and its optional packages stay optional. If the tool comes from a new package, add the package to an extra in pyproject.toml and to options._EXTRAS.
  3. Give the class a docstring whose first line describes the technique. The tables of the technique catalog in docs/catalog.md are made from these lines: write them again with uv run python docs/scripts/technique_catalog.py. A unit test checks that the catalog is up to date. If the technique (or a function) uses a tool from another package, end the description with a "Wraps:" section that names the tool by its import path, links to its documentation, and names its package:
Wraps:
    [`sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler.html)
    from scikit-learn.

List several tools as a list, each with what it is used for (such as "to classify"). A unit test checks that each tool in contents or tools is linked this way. 4. Make sure the technique learns only from the training rows, records what it did in the dataset's history, and uses the dataset's seed for anything random. 5. Add tests. Tests that use an optional package call requires (in tests/conftest.py) so that they are skipped where the package cannot be imported.

Examples in the README and the documentation are run by tests/test_docs.py. The comment lines after a print statement are its expected output.

The figures in the README are drawn by the breast cancer study in the README itself. If that study changes, draw them again (they are saved in docs/img):

uv run python docs/scripts/readme_figures.py

docs.title: Pull requests guidelines
docs.text:
Link to any related issue in the Pull Request message.

During the review, we recommend using fixups:

# SHA is the SHA of the commit you want to fix
git commit --fixup=SHA

Once all the changes are approved, you can squash your commits:

git rebase -i --autosquash main

And force-push:

git push -f

If this seems all too complicated, you can push or force-push each new commit, and we will squash them ourselves if needed, before merging.

docs.title: Style Guidelines
docs.text:
This package follows the Google Python Style Guide with two notable exceptions:

  1. It always adds spaces around "=". This not only violates the Google guide, it violates PEP8, the foundational Python style guide from which all other resources are derived. I defy this strong, long-standing norm because I find it more readable. My brain and eyes have trouble seeing two separate objects when an equal sign is in the middle. I imagine that I am not alone in this accessibility issue. Further, as PEP8 itself notes, required spaces around equal signs are becoming increasing common with type annotations becoming part of best practices (and, as a result, signatures to classes, functions, and methods regularly include spaces around the equal signs). I realize that this will seem alien to many coders, but it is far easier on my eyes.
  2. I use some so-called "power features", primarily dunder methods, to make my interfaces easier to access and use. This is disfavored in the Google Python Style Guide because such code is often more difficult for others to read. To address that concern, I try to document and comment as to what the code is doing whenever I used any of the "power features" of Python.

Because of the first exception, the project does not use a code formatter (such as ruff format), which would remove those spaces.

docs.title: Idea File
docs.text: A project's settings are its idea (a chrisjen.Idea). You can pass them to Project.create as a dict, but a settings file keeps the design of a study apart from its code, so it is easy to read, change, and share with the data. This page shows how to write one and describes every setting of its "general" section. The advanced user guide lists the settings of the other sections. Every example on this page is run by the amos unit tests.

docs.title: Writing the file
docs.text:
A settings file is made of sections, and each section is a set of named settings. This one describes a project named "cancer" with two workers:

[general]
label = target
seed = 43

[cancer_project]
cancer_workers = explorer, analyst

[explorer]
techniques = summarize

[analyst]
steps = split, scale, model
split_techniques = stratified
scale_techniques = standard
model_techniques = logit

Pass the path to the file to Project.create:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sklearn.datasets

import amos

data = sklearn.datasets.load_breast_cancer(as_frame = True).frame
project = amos.Project.create("study.ini", item = data)
dataset = project.result
print(project.name, dataset.label, dataset.task, dataset.seed)
# cancer target classify 43
print(project.idea["analyst"]["steps"])
# ['split', 'scale', 'model']

The name of the project is the part before "_project" of the first section whose name ends in "_project". If there is none, it is the name of the first section other than "general" and "files". Pass name to Project.create to choose it yourself.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
The format of the file is found from its extension:

Format Extension Values ini .ini Text, which is converted for you (see below). TOML .toml TOML's own types. YAML .yaml or .yml YAML's own types. Reading YAML needs the pyyaml package. JSON .json JSON's own types, and text is converted as in an ini file. Python .py The file must define a dict named settings. Its values are used as they are.

Here are the same settings in TOML:

[general]
label = "target"
seed = 43

[cancer_project]
cancer_workers = ["explorer", "analyst"]

[explorer]
techniques = "summarize"

[analyst]
steps = ["split", "scale", "model"]
split_techniques = "stratified"
scale_techniques = "standard"
model_techniques = "logit"

in YAML:

general:
  label: target
  seed: 43
cancer_project:
  cancer_workers: [explorer, analyst]
explorer:
  techniques: summarize
analyst:
  steps: [split, scale, model]
  split_techniques: stratified
  scale_techniques: standard
  model_techniques: logit

in JSON:

{
  "general": {"label": "target", "seed": 43},
  "cancer_project": {"cancer_workers": ["explorer", "analyst"]},
  "explorer": {"techniques": "summarize"},
  "analyst": {
    "steps": ["split", "scale", "model"],
    "split_techniques": "stratified",
    "scale_techniques": "standard",
    "model_techniques": "logit"
  }
}

and in Python:

settings = {
    "general": {"label": "target", "seed": 43},
    "cancer_project": {"cancer_workers": ["explorer", "analyst"]},
    "explorer": {"techniques": "summarize"},
    "analyst": {
        "steps": ["split", "scale", "model"],
        "split_techniques": "stratified",
        "scale_techniques": "standard",
        "model_techniques": "logit",
    },
}

Each gives the same project:

paths = ["study.toml", "study.yaml", "study.json", "study.py"]
ideas = [amos.Project.create(path, item = data).idea for path in paths]
print(all(dict(idea) == dict(project.idea) for idea in ideas))
# True

docs.title: How ini values are converted
docs.text:
Every value in an ini file is text, so it is converted for you (and so is the text in a JSON file):

Value Becomes Example A whole number An int seed = 43 Any other number A float test_size = 0.25 "true" or "yes" (in any case) True use_gpu = true "false" or "no" (in any case) False use_gpu = false Items in square brackets A list, with each item converted n_estimators = [200, 1000] Items separated by a comma and a space (or a line break) A list, with each item converted steps = split, scale, model Anything else Text label = target

A few things follow from these rules:

  • A list needs a comma and a space (or a line break) between its items. "split,scale" is a single piece of text.
  • A list can go on over several lines, if each line but the last ends with a comma and the lines after the first are indented.
  • Commas inside brackets, parentheses, or quotes do not split text, so a condition such as state = not in ['GU', 'PR'] stays one piece of text.
  • A list of one item is written as the item alone. Every setting that takes a list (such as "groups" or "techniques") also takes one name.
  • Text that looks like a number, true, or false is converted, so an ini or JSON file cannot name a column "yes" or "2020". Use a TOML, YAML (with quotes), or Python file for those.
  • Names of settings are case sensitive, and % has no special meaning. Lines that start with # or ; are comments, and so is the rest of a line after a # that has spaces on both sides (as in label = won # the outcome).
[analyst]
steps = split, encode,  # the first two steps
    model

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section What it holds general Settings for the data and the whole project, described below. files Where the project keeps its files, and whether it exports its results after every run (see the settings reference). {name}_project The project. Its {name}_workers setting lists the workers, in order. A section named for a worker The worker's steps, techniques, and design (see the settings reference). {name}_parameters Parameters for the technique, step, or worker name (see Set parameters). feature_groups Groups of features, each named as a technique that keeps only its features (see Groups of features).

docs.title: The general section
docs.text:
The "general" section describes the data and how every technique treats it. Every setting in it is optional.

Setting Value Default Meaning label A column name None The column that models predict. task "classify" or "regress" Inferred from the label Whether models classify or regress the label. seed A whole number None Seed for every random process, which makes the results reproducible. groups A column name, or a list of them None Columns that identify groups of rows, which are not used as features. use_gpu true or false false Whether to fit the models that can use a GPU on an NVIDIA GPU. conserve_memory true or false false Whether every experiment keeps only the best combination's whole dataset while it tries them. pipeline The name of a pipeline None Fills in the settings of the analyst, critic, and artist for a kind of study.

The settings (except conserve_memory and pipeline, which are for the workers) are given to the Dataset that the project makes from your data:

  • If you pass data (such as a DataFrame or the path to a data file), the dataset is made with these settings.
  • If you pass a Dataset, it keeps its own label, task, seed, and groups, and the settings fill in only those it lacks. "use_gpu" replaces the dataset's own if it is set.
  • If the workflow loads its own data with a loader (such as load_file), "label", "task", and "groups" are the loader's default parameters, and "seed" is the dataset's seed. Parameters in the loader's own section take precedence.
settings = {
    "general": {"seed": 43},
    "cancer_project": {"cancer_workers": ["explorer"]},
    "explorer": {"techniques": "summarize"},
}
mine = amos.Dataset(data, label = "target", seed = 7)
project = amos.Project.create(settings, item = mine)
print(project.result.label, project.result.seed)
# target 7

docs.title: label
docs.text:
The name of the column that models predict. Splitters that stratify, models, metrics, and evaluators need it, so a project without a label can only describe and change the data. They raise an error that asks you to set it. The label stays in the data but is not a feature.

A loader's data may have a label of its own: set "label" in the loader's parameters to use another one for that loader.

age,court,reversed
31,state,yes
45,federal,no
52,state,no
38,state,yes
60,federal,no

settings = {
    "general": {"label": "reversed", "seed": 43},
    "cases_project": {"cases_workers": ["loader"]},
    "loader": {"techniques": "load_file"},
    "load_file_parameters": {"source": "cases.csv"},
}
project = amos.Project.create(settings)
print(project.result)
# Dataset(rows=5, columns=3, label='reversed', task='classify')

The values of the label can be anything, including "yes" and "no". Only the settings file is converted, not the data.

docs.title: task
docs.text:
"classify" or "regress". Without it, the task is inferred from the label:

  • A label of text, booleans, or categories is classified.
  • A label of whole numbers with 10 or fewer different values (such as 0 and 1, or ratings from 1 to 5) is classified.
  • A label of decimal numbers that are all whole and take only two values (such as 0.0 and 1.0) is classified.
  • Any other label is regressed.

Set "task" when the inference is wrong for your study, such as ratings that should be regressed:

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ratings = pd.DataFrame({"hours": rng.uniform(0, 10, 200)})
ratings["stars"] = np.clip(ratings["hours"] // 2 + 1, 1, 5).astype(int)
print(amos.Dataset(ratings, label = "stars").task)
# classify
settings = {
    "general": {"label": "stars", "task": "regress", "seed": 43},
    "ratings_project": {"ratings_workers": ["analyst"]},
    "analyst": {
        "steps": ["split", "model"],
        "split_techniques": "train_test",
        "model_techniques": "linear",
    },
}
project = amos.Project.create(settings, item = ratings)
print(project.result.task)
# regress

The task chooses the version of each technique (such as RandomForestClassifier or RandomForestRegressor) and the metrics that the scorecard reports. A model that can only do one task raises an error if the task is the other one.

docs.title: seed
docs.text:
A whole number that seeds every random process: splitting the data, sampling, models, searches, and so on. It is passed as random_state to every tool that accepts one, unless the tool's parameters set random_state themselves. With the same settings, data, and seed, a project gives the same results every time:

settings = {
    "general": {"label": "target", "seed": 43},
    "cancer_project": {"cancer_workers": ["analyst"]},
    "analyst": {
        "steps": ["split", "model"],
        "split_techniques": "stratified",
        "model_techniques": "random_forest",
    },
}
first = amos.Project.create(settings, item = data)
second = amos.Project.create(settings, item = data)
print(first.result.predictions.equals(second.result.predictions))
# True
print(first.result.history[-1]["parameters"]["random_state"])
# 43

Without a seed, random processes differ from run to run. Set one for any study you will report. (Models fitted on a GPU can still differ slightly from the same models fitted on a CPU; see Fitting models on a GPU.)

docs.title: groups
docs.text:
The names of columns that identify groups of rows, such as race, court, or judge. Groups stay in the data, but they are not features, so transformers and models do not use them. They are used by:

  • the fairness metrics (demographic_parity, equalized_odds, and equal_opportunity, and their "_ratio" versions), which compare the model's predictions across the first group,
  • fairness, which makes a table of how the model does for each group,
  • the scorecard, which adds fairness metrics for every branch,
  • fixest, which can use them as fixed effects and clusters, and
  • group_split, which keeps the rows of each value of the first group in the same set.
clinics = data.copy()
clinics["clinic"] = np.where(np.arange(len(clinics)) % 3 == 0, "north", "south")
settings = {
    "general": {"label": "target", "seed": 43, "groups": "clinic"},
    "cancer_project": {"cancer_workers": ["analyst", "critic"]},
    "analyst": {
        "steps": ["split", "scale", "model"],
        "split_techniques": "stratified",
        "scale_techniques": "standard",
        "model_techniques": "logit",
    },
    "critic": {"techniques": "fairness"},
}
project = amos.Project.create(settings, item = clinics)
print(project.result.groups, "clinic" in project.result.features)
# ['clinic'] False
print(list(project.result.tables["fairness"].index))
# ['north', 'south', 'difference', 'ratio']

Every group must be a column of the data, or an error names the missing ones. See Groups and fairness for more.

docs.title: use_gpu
docs.text:
Whether to fit the models that can use a GPU (xgboost, catboost, lightgbm, and tabpfn, and the same models when an inferer fits them) on an NVIDIA GPU. It is false unless the settings set it to true, so a project runs on the CPU unless it asks for a GPU:

[general]
label = target
seed = 43
use_gpu = true

If there is no GPU, or a model cannot be fitted on it, amos warns and fits the model on the CPU, so the same settings work on any computer. Every other technique runs on the CPU either way. It must be true or false, or an error is raised. See Fitting models on a GPU for the details, including how to keep one model on the CPU and which GPUs need older packages.

docs.title: conserve_memory
docs.text:
Whether every experiment (and contest or survey) keeps only what it still needs while it tries its combinations of techniques. An experiment normally keeps every combination's whole dataset, with its features and fitted model, until the last one is done, so that a regression_table can show every combination's model. With many combinations or a large dataset, that may not fit in memory. If it is true, an experiment keeps only the best dataset so far, so no more than two are in memory at once; its comparison table, scores, and branches (and so the scorecard) are the same, but a regression_table has only the winner's model.

[general]
label = target
conserve_memory = true

A worker's own setting wins over the general one, so one experiment can keep every dataset while the others conserve memory:

[analyst]
design = experiment
conserve_memory = false

docs.title: pipeline
docs.text:
The name of a pipeline: the settings of an analyst, a critic, and an artist for a kind of study, chosen so that you do not have to write them. A whole study can be four lines:

[general]
label = target
seed = 43
pipeline = classification

project = amos.Project.create("pipeline.ini", item = data)
print(project.name, project.idea["classification_project"])
# classification {'classification_workers': ['analyst', 'critic', 'artist']}
print(project.idea["analyst"]["steps"])
# ['split', 'impute', 'scale', 'encode', 'sample', 'model']
print(project.idea["analyst"]["model_techniques"])
# ['logit', 'random_forest', 'gradient_boosting', 'baseline']
print(project.idea["critic"], project.idea["artist"])
# {'techniques': ['stratified_k_fold', 'auto_evaluator']} {'techniques': ['auto_plot']}

Without a project section, one named for the pipeline is added, with the analyst, critic, and artist as its workers. A project section that lists its own workers keeps them, and the pipeline fills in only the analyst, critic, and artist among them. The pipeline also sets "task" (if it is not set) and the parameters of some techniques, and project.idea (and the exported "settings.json") has every setting that it filled in, so the methods are still on the record.

The steps whose techniques depend on the data are "auto" (see Choosing techniques automatically), so one pipeline adapts to the data when it runs. Missing values are filled (if there are any), categorical features are encoded by how many levels they have (dummy variables for a few, the mean label for many), and rare classes are balanced (if they are rare). Each choice and its reason is in a table:

result = project.result
print(result.tables["auto_imputer"].loc["none", "reason"])
# no feature has missing values
print(result.tables["auto_sampler"].loc["none", "reason"])
# the classes are balanced: the rarest has 60% of the rows of the most common
print(result.tables["analyst_comparison"].index[0])
# stratified_split > auto_impute > standard_scale > auto_encode > auto_sample > logit_model
print(result.tables["auto_evaluator"].loc["regression_table", "reason"])
# logit has no coefficients with standard errors

These are the pipelines:

Pipeline Task What its analyst does classification classify Compares logit, random_forest, gradient_boosting, and baseline in an experiment, by balanced accuracy, after balancing rare classes. regression regress Compares ridge, random_forest, gradient_boosting, and baseline in an experiment, by RMSE. count_regression regress Compares poisson, negative_binomial, a random forest and gradient boosting fitted for counts, and baseline in an experiment, by RMSE. classification_inference classify Fits logit_sm for two classes, ordinal_regression for ordered classes, or mnlogit for others, with auto_model. regression_inference regress Fits ols, or robust_regression if the errors have outliers, with auto_model. count_inference regress Fits poisson, negative_binomial for overdispersed counts, or zero_inflated_poisson for excess zeros, with auto_model. panel_classification classify Fits a fixest logit model with the groups as fixed effects, clustered by the first group. panel_regression regress Fits a fixest model with the groups as fixed effects, clustered by the first group.

In each, the critic cross-validates the model (stratified_k_fold or k_fold) and applies the evaluators that suit it with auto_evaluator (such as confusion for classes, regression_table for a model with coefficients and standard errors, shap_importance for a model of trees, and fairness for two classes with groups), and the artist draws the figures that suit it with auto_plot.

The pipelines that predict scale the numeric features and balance rare classes. The pipelines for inference ("inference" and "panel") do neither: they keep the coefficients in the units of the features and the real share of each class (balancing would distort the coefficients and their standard errors), and they encode each categorical feature against its first level, so its coefficients are differences from that level. The panel pipelines need "groups".

Every setting that you write yourself wins, so a pipeline is a starting point. Change what you need and keep the rest:

settings = {
    "general": {"label": "target", "seed": 43, "pipeline": "classification"},
    "analyst": {"model_techniques": ["logit", "random_forest"]},
    "random_forest_parameters": {"max_depth": 4},
}
project = amos.Project.create(settings, item = data)
print(project.idea["random_forest_parameters"])
# {'n_estimators': 300, 'max_depth': 4}
print(len(project.result.tables["analyst_comparison"]))
# 2

A worker's own section can also name a pipeline, which fills in only that worker (and its parameters), such as pipeline = classification_inference in the "critic" section. To see what a pipeline fills in, look at it in amos.pipelines.PIPELINES. Add a Pipeline to it to name one of your own:

print(amos.pipelines.PIPELINES["regression_inference"].analyst["steps"])
# ['split', 'impute', 'encode', 'model']
amos.pipelines.PIPELINES["quick"] = amos.Pipeline(
    name = "quick",
    task = "classify",
    description = "A logit model and its confusion matrix.",
    analyst = {
        "steps": ["split", "model"],
        "split_techniques": ["stratified"],
        "model_techniques": ["logit"],
    },
    critic = {"techniques": ["confusion"]},
    artist = {"techniques": ["confusion_heatmap"]},
)
settings = {"general": {"label": "target", "seed": 43, "pipeline": "quick"}}
quick = amos.Project.create(settings, item = data)
print(sorted(quick.result.figures))
# ['confusion_heatmap']
del amos.pipelines.PIPELINES["quick"]
