docs.title: auto
docs.text:
Techniques that choose other techniques to suit the data.

Name "auto" in place of a technique, and amos chooses the techniques that suit the data when the workflow reaches it. "auto" works in a step that fills missing values, encodes, samples, models, evaluates, or plots (the kind of step is found from its name, such as "impute", "encode", "sample", "model", or "plot", or from the name of a worker such as "critic" or "artist"), or name the chooser yourself: auto_imputer, auto_encoder, auto_sampler, auto_model, auto_evaluator, or auto_plot.

[analyst]
steps = split, impute, encode, sample, model
split_techniques = stratified
impute_techniques = auto
encode_techniques = auto
sample_techniques = auto
model_techniques = auto

[critic]
techniques = auto

[artist]
techniques = auto

Each chooser first profiles the real training rows (see profile): the balance of the classes, the distribution of a regression's errors, whether the label is counts, missing values, the kinds and scales of the features, and how collinear they are. It then rules out the techniques whose needs or assumptions the data does not meet, and records why in a table in the dataset's tables (named for the chooser, such as "auto_model"), with a row for each technique it considered. The profile and the choice are also in the dataset's history, so a paper can report how each technique was chosen.

Contents

Profile: what the training rows are like. profile: returns the profile of a dataset. resolve: tells each "auto" technique in a workflow which kind of technique to choose, from the name of its step or worker. Chooser: base class for techniques that choose other techniques. Auto: chooses the techniques of the step that it is in. AutoEncoder: encodes each categorical feature in the way that suits how many levels it has, and dates by their parts. AutoEvaluator: applies the evaluators that suit the task and the model. AutoImputer: fills missing values in the ways that suit the features, or not at all. AutoModel: rules out models whose assumptions the data does not meet, cross-validates the rest, and fits the best. AutoPlot: draws the figures that suit the data and the model. AutoSampler: chooses a sampler that suits the balance of the classes and the features, or none.

docs.text:
Bases: Chooser

Encodes each categorical feature in the way that suits it.

Models need numbers, so every feature of text or categories is encoded, each with the first of these that suits it (the levels of a feature are counted in the training rows):

  • one_hot for a feature with 15 levels or fewer ("levels"): a dummy variable for each level, which every model can use and whose coefficients are easy to read.
  • tfidf (with skrub) for free text: a feature with more levels whose typical value has 3 words or more. It encodes the words of each value.
  • target (with category_encoders) for a feature with more levels, if the label has two classes or is regressed: the mean label of each level, shrunk toward the overall mean for rare levels. Dummy variables for so many levels would make the data wide and each level rare.
  • count (with category_encoders) for a feature with more levels and a label of more classes (or none): how often each level is in the training rows.
  • one_hot with at most "levels" columns for a feature with more levels, if category_encoders is not installed. Its rarest levels share one column.

Dates are split into their parts (year, month, day, and so on) by date_parts, with skrub.

The table (named "auto_encoder") has a row for each encoder considered (or a row for "none"), with whether it was chosen and why (or why not). The history records the encoder of each feature.

def apply(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    choices: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    levels: int = _LEVELS,
    **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Encodes the categorical features and dates of `item`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to encode.
        choices: names of the encoders to choose from, in the order to
            prefer them, for every feature. Defaults to `None`, which uses
            those in `_ENCODERS` for each kind of feature.
        levels: most levels of a feature for dummy variables. Defaults to
            15.
        **kwargs: parameters for the encoders (such as "drop" for
            `one_hot`). Each encoder uses those it accepts.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if no encoder suits a feature.

    Returns:
        The dataset, with its categorical features and dates encoded.

    """
    found = profile(item)
    rows = _real_rows(item)
    counts = {
        column: int(item.data.loc[rows, column].nunique())
        for column in item.categoricals}
    encoders: dict[str, str] = {}
    reasons: dict[str, str] = {}
    for column in item.dates + item.categoricals:
        kind = (
            'dates' if column in item.dates
            else _feature_kind(item.data.loc[rows, column], levels))
        names = (
            _ENCODERS[kind] if choices is None
            else camina.listify(choices))
        tried = {name: _screen_encoder(name, kind, found) for name in names}
        chosen = next(
            (name for name, reason in tried.items() if reason is None),
            None)
        if chosen is None:
            message = (
                f'{self.name!r} found no encoder for {column!r}: '
                + '; '.join(f'{n} {r}' for n, r in tried.items()))
            raise ValueError(message)
        encoders[column] = chosen
        for name, reason in tried.items():
            if name == chosen:
                break
            reasons.setdefault(name, cast('str', reason))
    if not encoders:
        table = pd.DataFrame(
            {'chosen': [True],
             'reason': ['there are no categorical features or dates']},
            index = pd.Index(['none']))
        self._record(item, table, found, [])
        return item
    groups: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
    for column, name in encoders.items():
        groups.setdefault(name, []).append(column)
    for name, columns in groups.items():
        parameters = dict(kwargs)
        if any(counts.get(column, 0) > levels for column in columns):
            parameters.setdefault('max_categories', levels)
        _borrow(name)().apply(item, columns = columns, **parameters)
    explained = {
        name: _encoder_suits(name, columns, counts, levels, found)
        for name, columns in groups.items()}
    for name, reason in reasons.items():
        explained.setdefault(name, reason)
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {'chosen': [name in groups for name in explained],
         'reason': list(explained.values())},
        index = pd.Index(list(explained)))
    self._record(item, table, found, list(groups), encoders = encoders)
    return item

docs.title: AutoEvaluator(contents=None, name='', parameters=dict()) dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Chooser

Applies the evaluators that suit the task and the model.

It needs the predictions of a fitted model, and applies those of these that suit it, in this order:

  • scorecard, which compares every branch (or the model) on every metric.
  • classification_report and confusion, for a classified label.
  • regression_table, for a model that reports coefficients with standard errors (such as ols, logit_sm, or fixest), unless the data came from an experiment. The table would have a column for each of its models, and estimate the effects of each model without coefficients by refitting it many times.
  • feature_importance, for a model with its own importances (or coefficients).
  • permutation_importance, which works for any scikit-learn model, when there is no regression table (which describes the features better).
  • shap_importance, for a model made of trees (with shap installed).
  • fairness, for a label of two classes with groups (with fairlearn installed).

Apply it before auto_plot, which draws the importances it finds. Evaluators that cannot be applied are left out, with a warning, and the reason is in the table (named "auto_evaluator").

def apply(

    item: base.Dataset,
    choices: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Applies the evaluators that suit `item`.

        **kwargs: parameters for the evaluators (such as "n_repeats").

        message = f'{self.name!r} needs the predictions of a fitted model'

Bases: Chooser

Fills missing values in the ways that suit the features.

Features without missing values are left alone, and so is a dataset without any. The numeric features with missing values are filled by the first of these that suits them:

  • iterative_impute, if a numeric feature misses more than 5% of its values in the training rows, there are at least two numeric features, and there are no more than 10,000 training rows. It models each feature from the others, which keeps their relationships better than filling every gap with one value.
  • median_impute, which fills each gap with the median of the training rows, which skewed values and outliers do not pull as they pull the mean.

The categorical and boolean features are filled with their most common values by mode_impute.

The table (named "auto_imputer") has a row for each imputer considered (or a row for "none"), with whether it was chosen and why (or why not).

def apply(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    choices: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Fills the missing values of the features of `item`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to fill.
        choices: names of the imputers to choose from, in the order to
            prefer them. Defaults to `None`, which uses `_IMPUTERS`.
        **kwargs: parameters for the imputers. Each imputer uses those
            it accepts.

    Returns:
        The dataset, with its missing values filled.

    """
    found = profile(item)
    missing = [
        column for column in item.features
        if base._kind_of(item.data[column]) != 'dates'
        and bool(item.data[column].isna().any())]
    if not missing:
        table = pd.DataFrame(
            {'chosen': [True], 'reason': ['no feature has missing values']},
            index = pd.Index(['none']))
        self._record(item, table, found, [])
        return item
    shares = item.data.loc[_real_rows(item), missing].isna().mean()
    kinds = {column: base._kind_of(item.data[column]) for column in missing}
    numeric = [c for c in missing if kinds[c] == 'numerics']
    most = float(shares[numeric].max()) if numeric else 0.0
    names = list(_IMPUTERS) if choices is None else camina.listify(choices)
    left = list(missing)
    filled: list[str] = []
    explained: dict[str, str] = {}
    for name in names:
        reason = _screen_imputer(
            name, len(item.numerics), len(_real_rows(item)), most)
        if reason is None:
            imputer = cast('type[transformers.Imputer]', _borrow(name))
            fills = imputer.kinds
            columns = [c for c in left if kinds[c] in fills]
            if columns:
                _borrow(name)().apply(item, columns = columns, **kwargs)
                left = [c for c in left if c not in columns]
                filled.append(name)
                explained[name] = _imputer_suits(name, columns, shares)
                continue
            reason = (
                f'suits the data, but {_names(filled, "and")} filled '
                f'the features it fills' if filled
                else 'no feature that it fills has missing values')
        explained[name] = reason
    if left:
        warnings.warn(
            f'{self.name!r} could not fill {left}: none of {names} fills '
            f'them',
            stacklevel = 2)
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {'chosen': [name in filled for name in explained],
         'reason': list(explained.values())},
        index = pd.Index(list(explained)))
    self._record(item, table, found, filled)
    return item

docs.text:
Bases: Chooser

Fits the best of the models whose needs and assumptions the data meets.

The models it considers (in the order it prefers them) are in _MODELS, with what each needs and assumes. It rules out the models that cannot do the task or use the features (missing values, categorical features, more features than rows, or features on very different scales for models that need them on similar scales), whose package is not installed, or whose assumptions the data does not meet:

  • linear assumes normal errors and features that are not collinear, so it is ruled out when the residuals of a least squares fit are materially skewed or heavy-tailed, or a feature's variance inflation factor is above 10.
  • naive_bayes assumes normal, independent features.
  • poisson assumes counts whose variance equals their mean, so it is ruled out for overdispersed counts (and for a label that is not counts). negative_binomial is for overdispersed counts and zero_inflated_poisson for counts with more zeros than a Poisson model expects.
  • robust_regression is for continuous errors with outliers, and ordinal_regression for three or more ordered classes.
  • logit, ridge, lasso, svm, knn, and neural_network need features on similar scales (put a scaler before them).
  • svm, knn, and neural_network are ruled out for data that is too large, too small, or too wide for them.

It also knows the needs of ols (features that are not collinear), logit_sm and probit (two classes), and mnlogit (three or more classes), which report coefficients with standard errors, but it only considers them when they are named in "choices".

The first candidates of the rest are cross-validated on the training rows (with stratified_k_fold for classification and k_fold for regression), and scored with metric. The model with the best score is fitted to the training rows, or, if simplest is true, the simplest model whose score is within one standard error of the best (the one-standard-error rule), which is easier to interpret and less likely to overfit.

The table (named "auto_model") has a row for each model considered, with whether it was chosen, why it was ruled out (or what it suits), and its cross-validated score and standard error.

def apply(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    choices: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    candidates: int = 4,
    folds: int = 5,
    metric: str | None = None,
    *,
    simplest: bool = True,
    **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Chooses a model and fits it to the training rows of `item`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to model. It must have a label.
        choices: names of the models to choose from, in the order to
            prefer them. Defaults to `None`, which uses the models in
            `_MODELS` that can do the task.
        candidates: most models to cross-validate. Defaults to 4.
        folds: number of cross-validation folds. Defaults to 5. If it is
            less than 2 (or the rarest class has fewer than 2 rows), the
            first model that suits the data is chosen without
            cross-validation.
        metric: name of the metric to score each model with. Defaults to
            `None`, which uses "balanced_accuracy" for classification and
            "rmse" for regression.
        simplest: whether to choose the simplest model whose score is
            within one standard error of the best. Defaults to `True`.
        **kwargs: parameters for the models. Each model uses those it
            accepts.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the dataset has no label, or no model suits it.

    Returns:
        The dataset, with the chosen model fitted and its predictions.

    """
    if item.task is None:
        message = f'{self.name!r} needs a dataset with a label'
        raise ValueError(message)
    found = profile(item)
    names = (
        [n for n, t in _MODELS.items() if found.task in t.tasks]
        if choices is None else camina.listify(choices))
    reasons = {name: _screen_model(name, found) for name in names}
    suited = [name for name, reason in reasons.items() if reason is None]
    if not suited:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} found no model that suits the data: '
            + '; '.join(f'{n} {r}' for n, r in reasons.items()))
        raise ValueError(message)
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {'chosen': False, 'reason': [
            _suits(name, found) if reason is None else reason
            for name, reason in reasons.items()],
         'score': np.nan, 'standard_error': np.nan},
        index = pd.Index(list(reasons)))
    tried = suited[:max(candidates, 1)]
    for name in suited[len(tried):]:
        table.loc[name, 'reason'] = (
            f'suits the data, but only the first {len(tried)} were '
            f'cross-validated')
    chosen = tried[0]
    details: dict[str, Any] = {}
    splits = _splits(item, folds)
    if len(tried) > 1 and splits > 1:
        metric = metric or (
            'balanced_accuracy' if item.task == 'classify' else 'rmse')
        scores = {}
        for name in tried:
            try:
                scores[name] = _cross_validate(
                    item, name, metric, splits, kwargs)
            # Any error means that the model cannot be fitted to this
            # data, so it is left out (and the reason is kept).
            except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001
                table.loc[name, 'reason'] = f'could not be fitted: {error}'
                warnings.warn(
                    f'{self.name!r} left out {name!r}, which could not be '
                    f'fitted: {error}',
                    stacklevel = 2)
                continue
            table.loc[name, ['score', 'standard_error']] = scores[name]
        if not scores:
            message = f'{self.name!r} could not fit any of {tried}'
            raise ValueError(message)
        better = getattr(_borrow(metric), 'greater_is_better', True)
        chosen = _best(scores, better = better, simplest = simplest)
        details = {'metric': metric, 'folds': splits}
    table.loc[chosen, 'chosen'] = True
    _borrow(chosen)().apply(item, **kwargs)
    self._record(item, table, found, [chosen], **details)
    return item

Bases: Chooser

Draws the figures that suit the data and the model.

Before a model is fitted (or if "data" is true), it draws the data: the label, the numeric features (histograms, their correlations, box plots by class, and a pair plot if there are few), the categorical features, and where values are missing. After a model is fitted, it draws the model:

  • For classification, the confusion matrix and, if the model predicts probabilities, the ROC curve, the calibration curve (with enough test rows), and the precision-recall curve (if the classes are imbalanced, when it says more than the ROC curve).
  • For regression, the actual labels and the residuals against the predictions, and, for a model whose standard errors assume normal errors (such as ols), a Q-Q plot of the residuals and, for ols and glm, the influence of each row.
  • Coefficients with their confidence intervals, if there are any; the importance of the features, if the model has them; partial dependence for models that are not linear; SHAP values for models made of trees (with shap installed); a decision tree's splits; an explainable boosting model's shape functions; a hyperparameter search; and fairness across groups (with fairlearn installed).

Plots that cannot be drawn are left out, with a warning, and the reason is in the table (named "auto_plot").

Bases: Chooser

Chooses a sampler that suits the classes and the features, or none.

A regressed label, or classes that are already balanced (the rarest class has at least half the rows of the most common), are not resampled. Otherwise, the first of these that suits the data is applied:

  • random_under, if the rarest class has so many rows (10,000) that removing rows of the common classes still leaves plenty.
  • smote_tomek, if the classes overlap (most of the nearest neighbors of most rare rows are of other classes), since it removes pairs of rows from different classes that are each other's nearest neighbors after it adds rows.
  • smote, which adds rows between rare rows and their neighbors.
  • random_over, which duplicates rare rows. SMOTE and its variants need numeric features without missing values, mostly not binary (they make values between those of two rows, which a dummy variable cannot have), and at least 6 rows of the rarest class.

The table (named "auto_sampler") has a row for each sampler considered (or a row for "none"), with whether it was chosen and why (or why not).

def apply(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    choices: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Resamples the training rows of `item`, if they need it.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to resample.
        choices: names of the samplers to choose from, in the order to
            prefer them. Defaults to `None`, which uses `_SAMPLERS`.
        **kwargs: parameters for the sampler (such as
            "sampling_strategy"). Each sampler uses those it accepts.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the dataset has no label.

    Returns:
        The dataset, resampled if it needed to be.

    """
    if item.task is None:
        message = f'{self.name!r} needs a dataset with a label'
        raise ValueError(message)
    found = profile(item)
    skip = _no_sampling(found)
    if skip is not None:
        table = pd.DataFrame(
            {'chosen': [True], 'reason': [skip]},
            index = pd.Index(['none']))
        self._record(item, table, found, [])
        return item
    overlap = _overlap(item)
    names = (
        list(_SAMPLERS) if choices is None else camina.listify(choices))
    reasons = {
        name: _screen_sampler(name, found, overlap) for name in names}
    chosen = next(
        (name for name, reason in reasons.items() if reason is None),
        None)
    if chosen is None:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} found no sampler that suits the data: '
            + '; '.join(f'{n} {r}' for n, r in reasons.items()))
        raise ValueError(message)
    explained = {
        name: (
            _sampler_suits(name, found, overlap) if name == chosen
            else f'suits the data, but {chosen} is preferred'
            if reason is None else reason)
        for name, reason in reasons.items()}
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {'chosen': [name == chosen for name in reasons],
         'reason': list(explained.values())},
        index = pd.Index(list(reasons)))
    _borrow(chosen)().apply(item, **kwargs)
    self._record(item, table, found, [chosen])
    return item

def profile(item: base.Dataset) -> Profile:
    """Returns what the real training rows of `item` are like.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to profile.

    Returns:
        The profile of the training rows that a sampler did not make up.

    """
    rows = _real_rows(item)
    if len(rows) > _PROFILE_ROWS:
        generator = np.random.default_rng(item.seed)
        rows = pd.Index(generator.choice(
            rows.to_numpy(), size = _PROFILE_ROWS, replace = False))
    x = item.data.loc[rows, item.features]
    kinds = {column: base._kind_of(x[column]) for column in x.columns}
    numerics = [c for c, k in kinds.items() if k == 'numerics']
    booleans = [c for c, k in kinds.items() if k == 'booleans']
    categories = [
        c for c, k in kinds.items()
        if k == 'categoricals' and isinstance(x[c].dtype, pd.CategoricalDtype)]
    matrix = x[numerics + booleans].astype(float)
    binary = [c for c in matrix.columns if _is_binary(matrix[c])]
    continuous = matrix.drop(columns = binary)
    found = Profile(
        task = item.task,
        rows = len(rows),
        features = len(kinds),
        numerics = len(numerics),
        binaries = len(binary),
        categories = len(categories),
        text = len(kinds) - len(numerics) - len(booleans) - len(categories),
        missing = bool(x.isna().to_numpy().any()),
        unscaled = _unscaled(continuous),
        vif = _largest_vif(continuous),
        skewed = _skewed_share(continuous, len(binary)))
    if item.label is None:
        return found
    y = item.y.loc[rows]
    if item.task == 'classify':
        _profile_classes(found, y)
    elif item.task == 'regress':
        _profile_errors(found, y, matrix)
    return found

def resolve(worker: Any) -> None:
    """Tells each "auto" technique in a workflow which genre to choose from.

    The genre of an `Auto` technique in a step is found from the name of the
    step (such as "sample", "model", or "plot"). The genre of one that is a
    technique of a worker without steps is found from the name of the worker
    (such as "artist"). An `Auto` technique that already has a genre keeps
    it.

    Args:
        worker: a workflow (a `chrisjen.Worker`).

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the genre of an "auto" technique cannot be found from
            its name.

    """
    if not isinstance(worker, chrisjen.Worker):
        return
    for node in worker:
        if isinstance(node, chrisjen.Step):
            contents = node.contents
            if isinstance(contents, Auto) and contents.genre is None:
                step = str(node.name).removeprefix(f'{contents.name}_')
                contents.genre = _genre_of(step)
            else:
                resolve(contents)
        elif isinstance(node, Auto) and node.genre is None:
            node.genre = _genre_of(str(worker.name))
        else:
            resolve(node)

docs.title: Branch(label, steps, result, score=None, criterion=None, source=None) dataclass
docs.text:
One branch of an experiment: a combination of techniques and its result.

An experiment tries every combination of one technique from each step. Each combination is a branch. The winning dataset keeps a Branch for every one of them, so that a scorecard can compare them after the experiment.

A branch also refers to the whole dataset that it made (with its fitted model and features), which the experiment keeps in its results, so that a regression_table can estimate the effects of each branch's model. The reference is weak: it does not keep the dataset in memory, and copies and pickles of the branch do not have it. An experiment that conserves memory keeps only the winner's dataset, so the other branches have none.

Data and everything learned from it in a workflow.

A Dataset is the item that an amos workflow works on. It holds the data in a single pandas.DataFrame, the name of the column that models predict (the label), and the rows in the training and test sets. As a workflow runs, each technique adds what it learns: the fitted model, its predictions, metrics, tables, figures, and a record of every step in history.

The data stays in one DataFrame even after it is split. Transformers learn from the training rows and then change every row, so nothing is learned from the test rows, and every row keeps its original label in the index.

@classmethod
def create(
    cls,
    item: Any,
    *,
    label: str | None = None,
    task: str | None = None,
    seed: int | None = None,
    groups: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    use_gpu: bool | None = None) -> Dataset:
    """Returns a `Dataset` made from `item`.

    Args:
        item: a `Dataset`, a `pandas.DataFrame` or `Series`, a Polars
            `DataFrame` or `LazyFrame`, a `numpy` array, a `dict` of
            columns, the path to a data file in any format that `nagata`
            knows (see `loaders.LoadFile`), or an object with a `frame`
            attribute (such as a scikit-learn dataset loaded with
            `as_frame = True`).
        label: name of the label column. Defaults to `None`. If `item` has
            a `target` (as a scikit-learn dataset does), its name is used.
        task: "classify" or "regress". Defaults to `None`, in which case
            it is inferred from the label.
        seed: seed for every random process. Defaults to `None`.
        groups: names of the columns that identify groups of rows.
            Defaults to `None`.
        use_gpu: whether models that can be fitted on a GPU use one.
            Defaults to `None`, which is `False` for a new `Dataset`.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if `item` is a path and there is no file there.
        TypeError: if `item` cannot be made into a `Dataset`.
        ValueError: if `item` is a path to a file whose format is not
            known.

    Returns:
        A `Dataset`. If `item` is already a `Dataset`, it is returned
            with any of `label`, `task`, `seed`, and `groups` that it
            lacks, and with `use_gpu` if it is passed.

    """
    if isinstance(item, Dataset):
        if item.label is None and label is not None:
            item.label = label
            item.task = task or (
                item.infer_task() if item.has_label else None)
        if item.task is None and task is not None:
            item.task = task
        if item.seed is None:
            item.seed = seed
        if not item.groups and groups:
            item.groups = _validate_groups(groups, item.data, item.label)
        if use_gpu is not None:
            item.use_gpu = _validate_use_gpu(use_gpu)
        return item
    if isinstance(item, str | pathlib.Path):
        # `loaders` imports this module, so it is imported here. The file
        # is read as `load_file` reads it, with a clerk for the current
        # folder.
        from . import loaders  # noqa: PLC0415
        item = loaders.LoadFile().read(item)
    if type(item).__module__.startswith('polars'):
        # Polars is optional, so its frames are recognized by their module.
        # A `LazyFrame` is collected first.
        frame = item.collect() if hasattr(item, 'collect') else item
        data = frame.to_pandas()
    elif isinstance(item, pd.DataFrame):
        data = item
    elif isinstance(item, pd.Series):
        data = item.to_frame()
    # A scikit-learn dataset is a `dict`, so it is checked before other
    # mappings.
    elif isinstance(getattr(item, 'frame', None), pd.DataFrame):
        data = item.frame
        target = getattr(item, 'target', None)
        if label is None and isinstance(target, pd.Series):
            label = str(target.name)
    elif isinstance(item, np.ndarray | Mapping):
        data = pd.DataFrame(item)
    else:
        message = f'a Dataset cannot be made from {type(item).__name__}'
        raise TypeError(message)
    return cls(
        data = data,
        label = label,
        task = task,
        seed = seed,
        groups = camina.listify(groups),
        use_gpu = _validate_use_gpu(use_gpu))

Returns the task implied by the type of the label.

A label that is boolean, categorical, or text is classified. So is an integer label with options._CLASSIFY_THRESHOLD unique values or fewer (such as 0 and 1), or a label of whole numbers stored as floats with only two unique values. Any other label is regressed. Pass task to override this.

Returns:

Type Description str

"classify" or "regress".

Source code in src/amos/base.py 
def infer_task(self) -> str:
    """Returns the task implied by the type of the label.

    A label that is boolean, categorical, or text is classified. So is an
    integer label with `options._CLASSIFY_THRESHOLD` unique values or
    fewer (such as 0 and 1), or a label of whole numbers stored as floats
    with only two unique values. Any other label is regressed. Pass `task`
    to override this.

    Returns:
        "classify" or "regress".

    """
    label = self.y
    unique = label.nunique(dropna = True)
    if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(label.dtype):
        return 'classify'
    if pd.api.types.is_bool_dtype(label.dtype):
        return 'classify'
    if pd.api.types.is_integer_dtype(label.dtype):
        if unique <= options._CLASSIFY_THRESHOLD:
            return 'classify'
        return 'regress'
    values = label.dropna()
    if unique <= 2 and bool((values == values.round()).all()):  # noqa: PLR2004
        return 'classify'
    return 'regress'

def replace(self, data: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    """Replaces `data`, keeping `train` and `test` to the rows that remain.

    If the label was pending and `data` has it, the task is inferred from
    it (unless it was set).

    Args:
        data: the new data.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if the label was a column of the data and is not a
            column of `data`, or if a group is not a column of `data`.

    """
    if self.has_label and self.label not in data.columns:
        message = f'the label {self.label!r} is not a column of the data'
        raise KeyError(message)
    missing = [g for g in self.groups if g not in data.columns]
    if missing:
        message = f'the groups {missing} are not columns of the data'
        raise KeyError(message)
    self.data = data
    if self.task is None and self.has_label:
        self.task = self.infer_task()
    if self.train is not None:
        self.train = self.train[self.train.isin(data.index)]
    if self.test is not None:
        self.test = self.test[self.test.isin(data.index)]
    self.synthetic = self.synthetic[self.synthetic.isin(data.index)]

Samplers add or remove training rows. The test rows (and their index labels) are not changed. The new training rows are given new index labels: integers after the largest current label if the index is made of integers, and otherwise "resampled_0", "resampled_1", and so on. The first copy of each real row is real. Synthetic rows and any other copies are added to synthetic.

def resample(
    self,
    x: pd.DataFrame,
    y: Sequence[Any],
    origins: Sequence[int] | np.ndarray | None = None) -> None:
    """Replaces the training rows with `x` and `y`.

    Samplers add or remove training rows. The test rows (and their index
    labels) are not changed. The new training rows are given new index
    labels: integers after the largest current label if the index is made
    of integers, and otherwise "resampled_0", "resampled_1", and so on.
    The first copy of each real row is real. Synthetic rows and any other
    copies are added to `synthetic`.

    Args:
        x: features of the new training rows.
        y: labels of the new training rows.
        origins: for each new row, the position (in the training rows) of
            the row it copies, which gives it that row's groups, or -1 for
            a synthetic row, which has no groups. Defaults to `None`, in
            which case no new row has groups and every new row is real.

    """
    label = self._require_label()
    made_up = self._train_rows().isin(self.synthetic)
    rows = x.copy()
    rows[label] = np.asarray(y)
    if self.groups:
        training = self.data.loc[self._train_rows(), self.groups]
        positions = np.full(len(rows), -1) if origins is None else (
            np.asarray(origins))
        copied = positions >= 0
        for group in self.groups:
            values = pd.Series(
                pd.NA, index = rows.index, dtype = training[group].dtype)
            values[copied] = training[group].to_numpy()[positions[copied]]
            rows[group] = values
    rows.index = self._new_labels(len(rows))
    rows = rows[self.data.columns]
    test = self.data.loc[self._test_rows()] if self.is_split else None
    self.data = pd.concat([rows, test]) if test is not None else rows
    self.train = rows.index
    self.synthetic = rows.index[_made_up(origins, made_up, len(rows))]

def split(self, train: Iterable[Any], test: Iterable[Any]) -> None:
    """Sets the training and test rows.

    Args:
        train: index labels of the training rows.
        test: index labels of the test rows.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if a row is in both sets or a label is not in the data.

    """
    training, testing = pd.Index(train), pd.Index(test)
    if len(training.intersection(testing)) > 0:
        message = 'a row cannot be in both the training and test sets'
        raise ValueError(message)
    missing = training.append(testing).difference(self.data.index)
    if len(missing) > 0:
        message = f'{len(missing)} rows to split are not in the data'
        raise ValueError(message)
    self.train, self.test = training, testing

def update_features(
    self,
    columns: Sequence[str],
    values: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    """Replaces the feature `columns` with `values`.

    Transformers use this to swap the columns they were given for the
    columns they produce, which may have different names or a different
    number of columns (one-hot encoding, for example). The new columns
    take the place of the first column they replace, so the order of the
    other columns does not change.

    Args:
        columns: names of the columns to remove.
        values: the new columns, with the same index as `data`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if `values` has a different index from `data`, or if a
            new column has the same name as a column that is kept.

    """
    if not values.index.equals(self.data.index):
        message = 'the new columns must have the same index as the data'
        raise ValueError(message)
    removed = set(columns)
    kept = [c for c in self.data.columns if c not in removed]
    clashes = [c for c in values.columns if c in kept]
    if clashes:
        message = (
            f'the new columns {clashes} have the same names as columns '
            f'that are kept'
        )
        raise ValueError(message)
    place = min(
        (i for i, c in enumerate(self.data.columns) if c in removed),
        default = len(self.data.columns))
    before = [c for c in self.data.columns[:place] if c not in removed]
    after = [c for c in self.data.columns[place:] if c not in removed]
    self.data = pd.concat(
        [self.data[before], values, self.data[after]], axis = 1)

Bases: Technique, ABC

Base class for amos techniques, which work on a Dataset.

An operation is a chrisjen.Technique, so it is stored in the chrisjen.library under its snake case name and can be named in the settings of any worker or step. Each technique writes apply, and every call to it makes the item into a Dataset (if it is not one already), passes it to apply with the technique's parameters, and returns it (see _call_apply). The dataset is changed in place. Every operation adds an entry to the dataset's history.

Operation is a genre: its abstract subclasses (Loader, Cleaner, Munger, Merger, Shaper, Describer, Splitter, Transformer, Sampler, Model, Validator, Evaluator, Inferer, and Plot) are genres within it. To add a technique, subclass the genre that fits and write the method it requires, or set contents to the tool to wrap. To add a new kind of technique, subclass Operation and write apply. (Metrics are not operations: see amos.metrics.Metric.)

docs.title: cleaners
docs.text:
Techniques that clean data, usually before it is studied or analyzed.

These are techniques of the "wrangler" stage of a project. Each one removes (or keeps) rows or columns, or renames columns. Techniques that change what is in the columns are mungers (see the mungers module), those that add the columns of another table are mergers (see the mergers module), and those that rearrange the rows and columns are shapers (see the shapers module). Cleaners learn nothing from the data that could leak from the test rows into the training rows (they do not, for example, fill missing values with an average), so they are safe to use before the data is split. To fill missing values, use an imputer from the transformers module after splitting.

Contents

Cleaner: base class for techniques that clean data. DropColumns: removes columns. DropConstant: removes columns that have only one value. DropDuplicates: removes duplicate rows. DropMissing: removes rows with missing values. FilterRows: keeps the rows that match a query, or a condition for each column. KeepColumns: keeps only some columns (and the label). RenameColumns: renames columns.

Each parameter other than "query" is a column, and its value is a condition for that column, so "state = not in ['GU', 'PR']" keeps the rows whose state is not "GU" or "PR". def clean(
    self,
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    query: str | None = None,
    **conditions: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Keeps the rows that match `query` and every condition.

    Args:
        data: the data to clean.
        query: a `pandas` query, such as "age >= 18". Column names with
            spaces go inside backticks. Defaults to `None`.
        **conditions: a condition for each column, by its name (see the
            class docstring).

    Raises:
        KeyError: if a condition is for a column that is not in the data.

    Returns:
        The rows that match `query` and every condition. If there are
            neither, every row.

    """
    missing = [c for c in conditions if c not in data.columns]
    if missing:
        message = (
            f'the columns {missing} that filter_rows has conditions for '
            f'are not in the data'
        )
        raise KeyError(message)
    parts = [] if query is None else [str(query)]
    parts.extend(_condition_query(c, v) for c, v in conditions.items())
    if not parts:
        return data
    joined = ' and '.join(f'({p})' for p in parts)
    return data.query(utilities.quote_bare_values(joined, data))

    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,

            keeps every column.

def apply(self, item: base.Dataset, **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Renames the columns of `item`, including its label and groups.

    The kinds of the renamed columns (see `Dataset.kinds`) are kept.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to clean.
        **kwargs: parameters for `clean`.

    Returns:
        The cleaned dataset.

    """
    names = {
        **dict(kwargs.pop('names', None) or {}),
        **{str(k): str(v) for k, v in kwargs.items()}}
    # The label and groups are renamed before the data so that `replace`
    # finds them.
    special = [c for c in [item.label, *item.groups] if c in names]
    if special:
        item.data = item.data.rename(
            columns = {c: names[c] for c in special})
        item.groups = [names.get(g, g) for g in item.groups]
        if item.label in names:
            item.label = names[item.label]
    item.kinds = {names.get(c, c): k for c, k in item.kinds.items()}
    return super().apply(item, names = names)

docs.title: clerks
docs.text:
The file manager of a project, which keeps data and results outside it.

A project's code is usually kept in a folder of a "code" folder (such as "projects/code/my_study"), and amos keeps its data and results beside the "code" folder, in the "workspace" that holds it:

projects/                (the workspace)
    code/
        my_study/        (the project's code)
    data/
        crime/nibrs/     (a project's data, in its own subfolder)
    studies/
        my_study_2026-10-30_09-15-00/   (each run's results)

So data that many projects use is kept once, results are never mixed with the code, and neither has to be left out of a repository by hand. The workspace is options._DEFAULT_ROOT, if a package sets it; otherwise the folder named by the environment variable in options._WORKSPACE_VARIABLE ("AMOS_WORKSPACE"), if it is set; otherwise the folder that holds the nearest folder named options._CODE_FOLDER ("code") above the current folder; and otherwise the current folder itself.

Contents

Clerk: the file manager of a project. workspace: returns the folder that holds the data and results.

The file manager of a project, which keeps data and results outside it.

It is the clerk of a Project (a nagata.FileManager): loaders look for data files and save downloads in its input_folder, intermediate files are kept in its interim_folder, and Project.export saves each run in a folder of its output_folder named for the run. By default, these are the "data" and "studies" folders of the workspace (see workspace), so every project keeps its data and results in the same places, outside its code. A project's own data can be kept in a subfolder of the data folder (such as "crime/nibrs"), named by data_subfolder.

Each folder can be set in the "files" section of a project's settings (relative folders are in root_folder), and the folders are made if they do not exist.

def workspace(start: pathlib.Path | str | None = None) -> pathlib.Path:
    """Returns the folder that holds the data and results of projects.

    Args:
        start: the folder to look up from for a "code" folder. Defaults to
            `None`, which uses the current folder.

    Returns:
        `options._DEFAULT_ROOT`, if it is set; otherwise the folder named by
            the environment variable in `options._WORKSPACE_VARIABLE`, if it
            is set; otherwise the folder that holds the nearest folder named
            `options._CODE_FOLDER` at or above `start`; and otherwise
            `start`.

    """
    if options._DEFAULT_ROOT is not None:
        return pathlib.Path(options._DEFAULT_ROOT).expanduser()
    named = os.environ.get(options._WORKSPACE_VARIABLE)
    if named:
        return pathlib.Path(named).expanduser()
    folder = pathlib.Path(start or pathlib.Path.cwd()).resolve()
    for path in (folder, *folder.parents):
        if path.name == options._CODE_FOLDER:
            return path.parent
    return folder

docs.title: describers
docs.text:
Techniques that describe data with tables.

These are the techniques of the "explorer" stage of a project. Each one adds a table to the dataset's tables (under the technique's name) and leaves the data unchanged. They describe every row, so use them before the data is split or to describe the data as it was collected.

Contents

Describer: base class for techniques that describe data with a table. AssociationRules: rules of which values tend to appear in the same rows. Correlations: correlations between the numeric columns. Describe: the pandas description of every column. Frequencies: the count and share of each value of the categorical columns. KaplanMeier: the share of rows without an event over time (survival). LabelBalance: the count and share of each value of the label. MissingValues: the count and share of missing values in each column. Summarize: summary statistics of the numeric columns. survival_curves: fits a Kaplan-Meier estimator for each group. survival_steps: the steps of a Kaplan-Meier curve, with its confidence interval.

docs.text:
Bases: Describer

Rules of which values tend to appear in the same rows.

mlxtend's association rules, as in an analysis of shopping baskets: each row is a set of items, which are the values of the categorical columns (as "{column} = {value}") and the boolean columns that are true, and of the label if it is classified. The sets of up to max_len items in at least min_support of the rows are found with FP-growth, and each rule "antecedents, then consequents" is kept if its metric is at least min_threshold (by default, a confidence of 0.8: 80% of the rows with the antecedents also have the consequents). The table has a row for each rule, with mlxtend's measures of it, largest lift first (how many times more often the consequents appear with the antecedents than they do in every row).

Wraps
  • mlxtend.frequent_patterns.fpgrowth from mlxtend, for the sets of items.
  • mlxtend.frequent_patterns.association_rules from mlxtend, for the rules.

def describe(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    *,
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    min_support: float = 0.1,
    metric: str = 'confidence',
    min_threshold: float = 0.8,
    max_len: int | None = 3,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the association rules of the values of `columns`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to describe.
        columns: the columns whose values are items. Defaults to `None`,
            which uses the categorical and boolean features, and the
            label if it is classified.
        min_support: smallest share of the rows that a set of items must
            be in. Defaults to 0.1.
        metric: the measure that a rule must reach, such as "confidence",
            "lift", "leverage", or "conviction". Defaults to
            "confidence".
        min_threshold: smallest value of `metric` for a rule. Defaults to
            0.8.
        max_len: most items in a set (of the antecedents and consequents
            together), or `None` for any number. Defaults to 3.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if no set of items is in `min_support` of the rows.

    Returns:
        One row for each rule, with its "antecedents" and "consequents"
            (each joined by commas) and mlxtend's measures of it.

    """
    frequent = utilities.import_tool('mlxtend.frequent_patterns')
    if columns is None:
        columns = [*item.categoricals, *item.booleans]
        if item.label is not None and item.task == 'classify':
            columns.append(item.label)
    items = _items(item.data, utilities.select_columns(item.data, columns))
    found = frequent.fpgrowth(
        items, min_support = min_support, use_colnames = True,
        max_len = max_len)
    if found.empty:
        message = (
            f'no set of items is in {min_support:.0%} of the rows: lower '
            f'"min_support"')
        raise ValueError(message)
    rules = frequent.association_rules(
        found, len(items), metric = metric, min_threshold = min_threshold)
    for side in ('antecedents', 'consequents'):
        rules[side] = [', '.join(sorted(s)) for s in rules[side]]
    table: pd.DataFrame = rules.sort_values(
        ['lift', 'confidence'], ascending = False, kind = 'stable',
        ignore_index = True)
    return table

def describe(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    columns: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the count and share of each value in `columns`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to describe.
        columns: columns to count, or "all". Defaults to `None`, which
            (like "all") counts the categorical and boolean features,
            including the dummies of `set_kinds`.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        One row for each value of each column, with "column", "value",
            "count", and "share" columns.

    """
    if columns is None or columns == 'all':
        columns = item.categoricals + item.booleans
    elif isinstance(columns, str):
        columns = [columns]
    tables = []
    for column in columns:
        counts = item.data[column].value_counts(dropna = False)
        tables.append(pd.DataFrame({
            'column': column,
            'value': counts.index.astype(str),
            'count': counts.to_numpy(),
            'share': (counts / counts.sum()).to_numpy()}))
    if not tables:
        return pd.DataFrame(columns = ['column', 'value', 'count', 'share'])
    return pd.concat(tables, ignore_index = True)

def describe(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    event: str | None = None,
    group: str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the estimated survival at each time.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to describe. Its label is the time.
        event: name of the column that is 1 if the event happened.
            Defaults to `None`, which means every event was observed.
        group: name of a column of groups. Defaults to `None`, which
            makes one curve for every row.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        One row for each time in each group (0, each time with an event,
            and the last time), with "group", "time", "survival" (the
            share without the event), and "at_risk".

    """
    tables = []
    for name, curve in survival_curves(item, event, group).items():
        steps = survival_steps(curve)
        steps.insert(0, 'group', name)
        tables.append(steps[['group', 'time', 'survival', 'at_risk']])
    return pd.concat(tables, ignore_index = True)

def survival_curves(
    item: base.Dataset,
    event: str | None = None,
    group: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Returns a fitted Kaplan-Meier estimator for each group.

    `kaplan_meier` and `survival_curves` (in the plots) both use this.

    Wraps:
        [`statsmodels.duration.survfunc.SurvfuncRight`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.duration.survfunc.SurvfuncRight.html)
        from statsmodels.

    Args:
        item: the dataset. Its label is the time until the event.
        event: name of the column that is 1 if the event happened. Defaults
            to `None`, which means every event was observed.
        group: name of a column of groups. Defaults to `None`, which makes
            one estimate, called "all", for every row.

    Returns:
        The fitted statsmodels `SurvfuncRight` of each group, by its name.

    """
    survfunc = utilities.import_tool('statsmodels.api.SurvfuncRight')
    times = item.y.astype(float)
    if event is None:
        observed = pd.Series(1, index = item.data.index)
    else:
        observed = item.data[event].astype(int)
    if group is None:
        groups = {'all': item.data.index}
    else:
        groups = {
            str(name): rows
            for name, rows in item.data.groupby(group).groups.items()}
    return {
        name: survfunc(
            times.loc[rows].to_numpy(), observed.loc[rows].to_numpy(),
            title = name)
        for name, rows in groups.items()}

Returns the steps of a Kaplan-Meier curve from survival_curves.

The curve starts at a time of 0 and ends at the last time that a row was observed. The confidence interval is the usual 95% interval of the log of minus the log of the survival, with Greenwood's variance.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default curve Any

a fitted statsmodels SurvfuncRight.

required

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

Source code in src/amos/describers.py 
def survival_steps(curve: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the steps of a Kaplan-Meier curve from `survival_curves`.

    The curve starts at a time of 0 and ends at the last time that a row was
    observed. The confidence interval is the usual 95% interval of the log of
    minus the log of the survival, with Greenwood's variance.

    Args:
        curve: a fitted statsmodels `SurvfuncRight`.

    Returns:
        One row for each time (0, each time with an event, and the last time),
            with "time", "survival", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", and "at_risk"
            (the number of rows whose time is at least that time).

    """
    observed = np.sort(np.asarray(curve.time, dtype = float))
    events = np.asarray(curve.surv_times, dtype = float)
    survival = np.asarray(curve.surv_prob, dtype = float)
    at_risk = np.asarray(curve.n_risk, dtype = float)
    happened = np.asarray(curve.n_events, dtype = float)
    z = statistics.NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)
    with np.errstate(divide = 'ignore', invalid = 'ignore'):
        greenwood = np.cumsum(happened / (at_risk * (at_risk - happened)))
        logged = np.log(survival)
        spread = z * np.sqrt(greenwood) / -logged
        lower = np.exp(-np.exp(np.log(-logged) + spread))
        upper = np.exp(-np.exp(np.log(-logged) - spread))
    # Once every row at risk has had the event, the survival is surely 0.
    lower[survival == 0] = 0.0
    upper[survival == 0] = 0.0
    times = np.unique(np.concatenate([[0.0], events, observed[-1:]]))
    # Before the first event, nobody has had it. Afterward, each time takes
    # the step of the last event at or before it.
    steps = np.searchsorted(events, times, side = 'right')
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'time': times,
        'survival': np.concatenate([[1.0], survival])[steps],
        'ci_lower': np.concatenate([[1.0], lower])[steps],
        'ci_upper': np.concatenate([[1.0], upper])[steps],
        'at_risk': len(observed) - np.searchsorted(observed, times)})

docs.title: evaluators
docs.text:
Techniques that evaluate a fitted model with tables.

These are techniques of the "critic" stage. Each one adds a table to the dataset's tables (under the technique's name). Most evaluate the model on the test rows (or on every row, if the data has not been split). factor_analysis and pca instead describe the features that the model learned from, so they work in any stage.

Contents

Evaluator: base class for techniques that evaluate a model with a table. BiasVariance: the model's expected error, as its bias and variance. ClassificationReport: precision, recall, and f1 for each class. Confusion: how many rows of each class were predicted to be each class. Conformal: prediction intervals (or sets) with a known rate of coverage. ExplainWeights: eli5's explanation of the weights of the features. FactorAnalysis: the hidden factors that explain the correlations of the features. Fairness: how the model does for each group, and the gaps between them. FeatureImportance: the importance that the model gives each feature. PCA: how much of the variance of the features each principal component has. PermutationImportance: how much the score drops when each feature is shuffled. RegressionTable: the coefficients (or average marginal effects) of every model side by side, with their standard errors and cross-validated metrics, ready to publish like a scorecard. Scorecard: every standard metric for every branch of an analysis, ready to publish as csv, Markdown, LaTeX, HTML, Word, or an image. ShapImportance: the mean absolute SHAP value of each feature.

docs.title: BiasVariance(contents=None, name='', parameters=dict()) dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Evaluator

The model's expected error on the test rows, as its bias and variance.

mlxtend's bias-variance decomposition: copies of the model are fitted to rounds bootstrap samples of the training rows, and each predicts the test rows. The expected loss is their mean loss: the share of rows misclassified (0-1 loss), for a classifier, or the mean squared error. The bias is the loss of their main prediction (the most common class, or the mean), and the variance is how far the copies' predictions are from it. A model with a large bias underfits; one with a large variance overfits. The table has one row, with the "loss", "expected_loss", "bias", and "variance".

Wraps

mlxtend.evaluate.bias_variance_decomp from mlxtend.

def evaluate(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    rounds: int = 100,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the expected loss of the model, and its bias and variance.

    Args:
        item: the dataset with a fitted scikit-learn model and test rows.
        rounds: number of bootstrap samples (and copies of the model).
            Defaults to 100.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        TypeError: if the model is not a scikit-learn estimator.
        ValueError: if the data is not split.

    Returns:
        One row, with the loss and its parts.

    """
    evaluate = utilities.import_tool('mlxtend.evaluate')
    sklearn = importlib.import_module('sklearn.base')
    if not item.is_split:
        message = 'bias_variance needs test rows: split the data first'
        raise ValueError(message)
    model = _model(item)
    names = list(
        utilities.feature_names(model, item.data.columns) or item.features)
    y_train, y_test = item.y_train, item.y_test
    if isinstance(model, models.LabelCoded):
        model = model.estimator
    if item.task == 'classify':
        # mlxtend counts the predictions of each class by its number.
        positions = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(item.classes)}
        y_train, y_test = y_train.map(positions), y_test.map(positions)
    if not isinstance(model, sklearn.BaseEstimator):
        message = (
            f'bias_variance needs a scikit-learn model, not a '
            f'{type(model).__name__}')
        raise TypeError(message)
    loss = '0-1_loss' if item.task == 'classify' else 'mse'
    expected, bias, variance = evaluate.bias_variance_decomp(
        sklearn.clone(model),
        item.x_train[names].to_numpy(),
        y_train.to_numpy(),
        item.x_test[names].to_numpy(),
        y_test.to_numpy(),
        loss = loss,
        num_rounds = rounds,
        random_seed = item.seed)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'loss': [loss],
        'expected_loss': [float(expected)],
        'bias': [float(bias)],
        'variance': [float(variance)]})

Bases: Evaluator

Prediction intervals (or sets) with a known rate of coverage.

Conformal prediction turns any model's predictions into intervals (for regression) or sets of classes (for classification) that contain the true value for at least a chosen share of rows ("confidence", 90% by default), without assumptions about the data's distribution. It wraps MAPIE's cross-conformal methods, which refit copies of the model on folds of the training rows ("cv", 5 by default). The table has a row for each test row. The share of rows covered ("coverage") and the mean width of the intervals ("interval_width") or size of the sets ("set_size") are stored in the dataset's metrics.

Wraps

  • mapie.regression.CrossConformalRegressor from MAPIE, to regress.

def apply(self, item: base.Dataset, **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Adds the table and stores the coverage and width (or set size).

    Args:
        item: the dataset with a fitted model.
        **kwargs: parameters for `evaluate`.

    Returns:
        The dataset, with the table in `tables` and the coverage in
            `metrics`.

    """
    super().apply(item, **kwargs)
    table = item.tables[self.name]
    item.metrics['coverage'] = float(table['covered'].mean())
    if 'lower' in table.columns:
        item.metrics['interval_width'] = float(
            (table['upper'] - table['lower']).mean())
    else:
        item.metrics['set_size'] = float(table['size'].mean())
    return item

def evaluate(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    confidence: float = 0.9,
    cv: int = 5,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the interval (or set) of each test row.

    Args:
        item: the dataset with a fitted model.
        confidence: share of rows that the intervals should cover.
            Defaults to 0.9.
        cv: number of folds of the training rows. Defaults to 5.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        One row for each test row, with "actual", "prediction", "lower"
            and "upper" (or "set" and "size"), and "covered".

    """
    sklearn_base = importlib.import_module('sklearn.base')
    model = _model(item)
    columns = (
        utilities.feature_names(model, item.data.columns) or item.features)
    rows = item.y_test.index if item.is_split else item.data.index
    train = item.y_train.index
    estimator = sklearn_base.clone(model)
    actual = item.y.loc[rows]
    if item.task == 'regress':
        regression = utilities.import_tool('mapie.regression')
        conformal = regression.CrossConformalRegressor(
            estimator,
            confidence_level = confidence,
            cv = cv,
            random_state = item.seed)
        conformal.fit_conformalize(
            item.data.loc[train, columns], item.y_train)
        predicted, intervals = conformal.predict_interval(
            item.data.loc[rows, columns])
        lower = intervals[:, 0, 0]
        upper = intervals[:, 1, 0]
        return pd.DataFrame({
            'actual': actual,
            'prediction': predicted,
            'lower': lower,
            'upper': upper,
            'covered': (actual >= lower) & (actual <= upper)},
            index = rows)
    classification = utilities.import_tool('mapie.classification')
    conformal = classification.CrossConformalClassifier(
        estimator,
        confidence_level = confidence,
        cv = cv,
        random_state = item.seed)
    conformal.fit_conformalize(item.data.loc[train, columns], item.y_train)
    predicted, sets = conformal.predict_set(item.data.loc[rows, columns])
    classes = np.unique(np.asarray(item.y_train))
    members = [
        [c for c, inside in zip(classes, row, strict = True) if inside]
        for row in sets[:, :, 0]]
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'actual': actual,
        'prediction': predicted,
        'set': [', '.join(str(c) for c in m) for m in members],
        'size': [len(m) for m in members],
        'covered': [
            a in m for a, m in zip(actual, members, strict = True)]},
        index = rows)

def apply(self, item: base.Dataset, **kwargs: Any) -> base.Dataset:
    """Adds the table from `evaluate` to the tables of `item`.

def evaluate(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    top: int = 20,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns eli5's table of the model's weights.

    Args:
        item: the dataset with a fitted model.
        top: most weights to list. Defaults to 20.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if eli5 cannot explain the model.

    Returns:
        eli5's table of weights.

    """
    eli5 = utilities.import_tool('eli5')
    model = _model(item)
    if isinstance(model, models.LabelCoded):
        model = model.estimator
    names = [str(n) for n in (
        utilities.feature_names(model, item.data.columns)
        or item.features)]
    table: pd.DataFrame | None = eli5.explain_weights_df(
        model, feature_names = names, top = top)
    if table is None:
        message = (
            f'eli5 cannot explain the weights of {type(model).__name__}')
        raise ValueError(message)
    return table

def evaluate(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    *,
    factors: int | None = None,
    method: str = 'pa',
    rotation: str | None = 'varimax',
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the loading of each feature on each factor.

    Args:
        item: the dataset.
        factors: number of factors. Defaults to `None`, which uses
            Kaiser's rule.
        method: "pa" (principal axes) or "ml" (maximum likelihood).
            Defaults to "pa".
        rotation: how statsmodels rotates the loadings, such as
            "varimax", "quartimax", "promax", or "oblimin", or `None`
            (or "none") to leave them unrotated. Defaults to "varimax".
        columns: the columns to analyze. Defaults to `None`, which uses
            the numeric and boolean features.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        One row for each feature, with a "factor_{n}" column for each
            factor, "communality", and "uniqueness".

    """
    factor = utilities.import_tool('statsmodels.multivariate.factor')
    data = _numbers(item, columns, self.name)
    count = factors or _kaiser(data)
    results = factor.Factor(
        data, n_factor = count, method = method, missing = 'drop').fit()
    if rotation not in {None, 'none'} and count > 1:
        results.rotate(rotation)
    names = [f'factor_{n}' for n in range(1, count + 1)]
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        np.asarray(results.loadings), index = data.columns, columns = names)
    table['communality'] = np.asarray(results.communality)
    table['uniqueness'] = np.asarray(results.uniqueness)
    return table

def evaluate(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    group: str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the metrics of each group and the gaps between them.

    Args:
        item: the dataset with a fitted classifier.
        group: name of the column of groups. Defaults to `None`, which
            uses the dataset's first group.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        One row for each group, then "difference" and "ratio" rows.

    """
    fairness = utilities.import_tool('fairlearn.metrics')
    scores = importlib.import_module('sklearn.metrics')
    column = metrics_._group(item, group, self.name)
    y_true, y_pred = _observed(item)
    y_true, y_pred = metrics_._positive(item, y_true, y_pred, self.name)
    frame = fairness.MetricFrame(
        metrics = {
            'count': fairness.count,
            'selection_rate': fairness.selection_rate,
            'accuracy': scores.accuracy_score,
            'true_positive_rate': fairness.true_positive_rate,
            'false_positive_rate': fairness.false_positive_rate},
        y_true = y_true,
        y_pred = y_pred,
        sensitive_features = item.data.loc[y_true.index, column])
    table: pd.DataFrame = frame.by_group.copy()
    table.index = table.index.astype(str)
    table.loc['difference'] = frame.difference()
    table.loc['ratio'] = frame.ratio()
    table.index.name = column
    return table

def evaluate(self, item: base.Dataset, **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the importance of each feature, largest first.

    Args:
        item: the dataset with a fitted model.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the model does not report the importance of its
            features.

    Returns:
        One row for each feature, with an "importance" column.

    """
    model = _model(item)
    importances = getattr(model, 'feature_importances_', None)
    if importances is None and hasattr(model, 'term_importances'):
        # An Explainable Boosting Machine reports the importance of each
        # term (a feature or a pair of features).
        return _importance_table(
            [str(n) for n in model.term_names_],
            np.asarray(model.term_importances()))
    if importances is None:
        coefficients = getattr(model, 'coef_', None)
        if coefficients is None:
            message = (
                f'{type(model).__name__} does not report the importance of '
                f'its features: use permutation_importance instead'
            )
            raise ValueError(message)
        importances = np.abs(np.atleast_2d(coefficients)).mean(axis = 0)
    features = (
        utilities.feature_names(model, item.data.columns) or item.features)
    coefficients = getattr(model, 'coefficients', None)
    if len(np.ravel(importances)) != len(features) and callable(coefficients):
        # A model that drops features (such as pyfixest's, which drops
        # collinear ones) has a coefficient only for the others.
        table = coefficients().dropna(subset = ['coefficient'])
        kept = [f for f in features if f in table.index]
        return _importance_table(
            kept, np.abs(table.loc[kept, 'coefficient'].to_numpy(float)))
    return _importance_table(features, np.asarray(importances))

def evaluate(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    *,
    components: int | None = None,
    standardize: bool = True,
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the eigenvalue and share of the variance of each component.

    Args:
        item: the dataset.
        components: number of components. Defaults to `None`, which uses
            one for each column.
        standardize: whether to give each column a standard deviation of
            1 first, so that the columns with the largest values do not
            dominate. Defaults to `True`.
        columns: the columns to analyze. Defaults to `None`, which uses
            the numeric and boolean features.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        One row for each component, with its "eigenvalue" (of the
            correlations of the columns, or of their covariances if
            `standardize` is `False`), the "share" of the variance that
            it explains, and the "cumulative" share of it and the
            components before it.

    """
    pca = utilities.import_tool('statsmodels.multivariate.pca.PCA')
    data = _numbers(item, columns, self.name)
    results = pca(
        data,
        ncomp = components,
        standardize = standardize,
        missing = 'drop-row')
    count = len(results.eigenvals)
    names = [f'component_{n}' for n in range(1, count + 1)]
    # statsmodels' eigenvalues are multiplied by the number of rows, and
    # the R² of the first n components is the share of the variance that
    # they explain together.
    rows = len(results.factors)
    cumulative = np.asarray(results.rsquare)[1:count + 1]
    item.tables[f'{self.name}_loadings'] = pd.DataFrame(
        np.asarray(results.loadings), index = data.columns, columns = names)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'eigenvalue': np.asarray(results.eigenvals) / rows,
        'share': np.diff(cumulative, prepend = 0.0),
        'cumulative': cumulative},
        index = names)

def evaluate(
    self,
    item: base.Dataset,
    n_repeats: int = 10,
    scoring: str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the mean and standard deviation of each feature's importance.

    Args:
        item: the dataset with a fitted model.
        n_repeats: times to shuffle each feature. Defaults to 10.
        scoring: scikit-learn scorer. Defaults to `None`, which uses
            "accuracy" or "r2" for the task.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        One row for each feature, with "importance" and "std" columns,
            largest first.

    """
    inspection = importlib.import_module('sklearn.inspection')
    x = item.x_test if item.is_split else item.x
    y = item.y.loc[x.index]
    if scoring is None:
        scoring = 'accuracy' if item.task == 'classify' else 'r2'
    model = _model(item)
    others = _other_columns(model, item)
    if others or not hasattr(model, '__sklearn_tags__'):
        model = _GivenColumns(model, item.data.loc[x.index, others], item.task)
    result = inspection.permutation_importance(
        model,
        x,
        y,
        n_repeats = n_repeats,
        scoring = scoring,
        random_state = item.seed)
    table = _importance_table(list(x.columns), result.importances_mean)
    table['std'] = pd.Series(
        result.importances_std, index = list(x.columns))
    return table

docs.text:
Bases: _Published, Evaluator

The estimates of every model side by side, ready to publish.

Like the regression tables of Stata, R, and statsmodels, it has a column for each model and two rows for each feature: its estimate, with stars for its p-value, and below it, its standard error in parentheses. The models are the branches of the most recent experiment, or the final model if the data did not come from one. Rows below the estimates describe each model: the kind of estimates, the number of observations that it learned from, and its cross-validated metrics.

A model that reports its coefficients and their statistics (the statsmodels and pyfixest models, such as ols, logit_sm, glm, and fixest) is shown with them. Every other model is shown with the average marginal effect (AME) of each feature: the average change in the prediction (or in the predicted probability of each class, for a classifier) for a one-unit increase in the feature. These are models without coefficients (such as random_forest or xgboost) and the scikit-learn linear models, whose coefficients have no standard errors. The AME of a linear regression is its coefficient. For each training row, a feature is moved up and down by "step" of its standard deviations (0.1 by default), or from its lower to its higher value if it has only two. The standard error and 95% confidence interval of an AME come from refitting the model to "simulations" bootstrap samples of the training rows (100 by default), and its p-value comes from the normal distribution. Set "marginal" to true to show marginal effects for every model, which puts every column on the same scale.

Features that form a set, such as the dummy variables of one category with its reference left out (a victim's relationship to an offender: "family", "partner", or "stranger", against "unknown"), cannot be moved one at a time: setting "family" to 1 in a row whose "stranger" is 1 makes a row that cannot happen. Name them in "sets" (in settings, as "family, partner, stranger; under_12, teen", with sets separated by semicolons) and the AME of each member is the average change in the prediction from the reference (every member 0) to that member alone (it 1, the others 0). The members of a set must have two values each, and members that are not features of a model are left out of its set.

The metrics are cross-validated on the training rows, never scored on the rows that the model learned from. They are the "cv_{metric}" metrics of a validator that the analysis already ran, or else they come from the validator named by "validator" (stratified_k_fold to classify and k_fold to regress, by default).

A marginal effect describes the model, not the world. It is the model's estimated effect if every other feature is held fixed, so it is only causal if the features are (see the inferers to estimate a causal effect). It can mislead when features are correlated, since moving one while holding the others fixed makes rows unlike any real one. The bootstrap treats rows as independent, so its standard errors are too small for rows that are correlated within groups or over time.

The estimates are stored in the dataset's tables under the technique's name, with one row for each model and feature, and the rows below them are stored as "{name}_statistics". The table can be saved in the same formats as a scorecard (csv, Markdown, LaTeX, HTML, Word, or an image). In the "stata" style (the default), Word documents, images, and to_text look like Stata's output of regress: a block for each model, with a description of the model and its statistics at the top and a table of its estimates below them ("Coef." or "dy/dx", "Std. Err.", "t" or "z", its p-value, and its 95% confidence interval), set in a monospaced font between rules. In the "columns" style, they put the models side by side, as csv, Markdown, LaTeX, and HTML always do (like Stata's esttab). Make one from a dataset, an applied project, or several datasets with create.

Wraps
  • sklearn.base.clone from scikit-learn, to refit each model to bootstrap samples.
  • scipy.stats.norm from SciPy, for the p-values of marginal effects.
  • docx.Document from python-docx, for to_word.
  • matplotlib.figure.Figure from matplotlib, for to_image.
